u1.intro: Multiple-choice questions 17-24 and free-response question 1 allow a graphing calculator; all other questions are no calculator.

mc.stem:
Questions 1-2 refer to the following.

A ball is dropped from the top of a tall building. The table gives s(t), the distance in meters that the ball has fallen t seconds after it is dropped, at times near t = 3.
t (seconds) · s(t) (meters)
2.9 · 41.209
2.99 · 43.80649
3 · 44.1
3.01 · 44.39449
3.1 · 47.089

parts.q:
Which of the following is the best estimate, in meters per second, of the ball's speed at the instant t = 3 that the table supports?
(A) 44.1
(B) 14.7
(C) 29.4
(D) 29.89
parts.a: (C). The speed at an instant is the limit of average speeds over shorter and shorter intervals that contain t = 3. Over [2.99, 3] the average speed is (44.1 − 43.80649)/0.01 = 29.351, and over [3, 3.01] it is (44.39449 − 44.1)/0.01 = 29.449. The averages over [2.9, 3] (28.91) and [3, 3.1] (29.89) show the same pattern: the averages from the left rise and those from the right fall as the intervals shrink, closing in on about 29.4. (A) is s(3), the distance fallen, not a rate. (B) is s(3)/3, the average speed over the whole fall from t = 0 to t = 3, not the speed at t = 3. (D) is the average speed over [3, 3.1], the widest interval in the table; the narrower intervals give better estimates.
parts.n: CHA-1.A.3 (topic 1.1), LIM-1.C.5 (topic 1.4); skill 2.B. Thinking: turn the table into average rates over shrinking intervals on both sides and read off the value they approach. Trap: (B), the average speed over the whole fall.

parts.q:
A student says, "The speed at t = 3 is the average speed over the interval from t = 3 to t = 3. That is (s(3) − s(3))/(3 − 3), and in zero time the ball covers zero distance, so its speed at t = 3 is 0." Which of the following best evaluates the student's reasoning?
(A) It is wrong: the quotient is 0/0, which is undefined; the speed at t = 3 is the limit of the average speeds, about 29.4.
(B) It is right: an instant has no length, so no distance is covered in it, and the ball's speed at any single instant must be 0.
(C) It is wrong: since the average speed over [3, 3] is undefined, the ball has no speed at t = 3; speed is defined only over an interval.
(D) It is wrong: the speed at t = 3 is the average speed over [0, 3], which is s(3)/3 = 14.7, because the ball starts from rest.
parts.a: (A). An average speed divides the change in distance by the change in time, and over [3, 3] both changes are 0, so the quotient is 0/0: undefined, not 0. Calculus defines the speed at an instant as the limit of average speeds over intervals that shrink toward t = 3, and the table shows those averages approaching about 29.4 meters per second. (B) accepts the 0/0 as 0; the ball is clearly moving at t = 3, since it falls about 0.29 meter in the next hundredth of a second. (C) sees that the quotient is undefined but wrongly concludes that no instantaneous rate exists; the limit of average rates is exactly what gives one. (D) replaces the rate at an instant with the average over the whole fall, which is only half the speed at t = 3.
parts.n: CHA-1.A.2, CHA-1.A.3 (topic 1.1); skill 3.E. Thinking: see that an average rate over a zero-length interval is undefined, and that a limit of average rates is what defines a rate at an instant. Trap: (C), 'undefined quotient, so no speed at an instant'.

mc.stem:
Questions 3-5 refer to the following.

Let f be the function defined by f(x) = sin(π/x) for x ≠ 0. A student evaluates f at six inputs near 0 and records the results.
x · f(x)
−0.1 · 0
−0.01 · 0
−0.001 · 0
0.001 · 0
0.01 · 0
0.1 · 0
The student concludes that $\lim_{x \to 0} f(x) = 0$.

parts.q:
Which of the following best evaluates the student's conclusion?
(A) It is correct: the values from the left and from the right agree, and they are all 0, so the limit is 0.
(B) It is wrong only because f(0) is undefined; a limit at x = 0 cannot exist unless f(0) exists.
(C) It is correct, because sin(π/x) stays between −1 and 1, and a bounded function has a limit at every point.
(D) It is wrong: each input makes π/x a multiple of π; at other inputs near 0, f(x) = 1, so there is no limit.
parts.a: (D). Every input in the table has the form ±1/10ᵏ, so π/x = ±10ᵏπ is a whole multiple of π and the sine is 0 by the choice of inputs, not because f is settling down. At x = 2/401, for example, π/x = 200.5π and f(x) = sin(200.5π) = 1, and such inputs occur as close to 0 as you like. Since f keeps taking the values 0 and 1 (indeed every value from −1 to 1) arbitrarily close to x = 0, the limit does not exist; it fails by oscillation. (A) trusts a table built from special inputs; agreement at six points cannot show what f does at the points between them. (B) confuses the limit with the function value: a limit never depends on f(0), and many limits exist where f is undefined. (C) is false: boundedness does not force a limit, and this function is the standard example of a bounded function with no limit.
parts.n: LIM-1.C.4, LIM-1.C.5 (topics 1.3, 1.4); skill 3.G. Thinking: ask whether the table's inputs are typical or special before trusting the pattern. Trap: (A), agreement from both sides in a table taken as proof.

parts.q:
Which of the following sets of inputs, added to the table, would show that the student's conclusion is wrong?
(A) x = 0.0001, 0.00001 and 0.000001
(B) x = 2/401, 2/4001 and 2/40001
(C) x = 0.5, 0.25 and 0.125
(D) x = 1/3, 1/30 and 1/300
parts.a: (B). At x = 2/401, 2/4001 and 2/40001, π/x equals 200.5π, 2000.5π and 20000.5π, so f(x) = 1 each time, while the table's inputs, just as close to 0, give 0. Two different values taken arbitrarily close to 0 show the limit does not exist. (A) moves closer to 0, but π/x = 10000π, 100000π, 1000000π is still a multiple of π, so every value is again 0 and the misleading pattern continues. (C) halves the distance to 0, but π/x = 2π, 4π, 8π, so every value is 0 again (and these inputs are not even close to 0). (D) looks like a fresh sequence, but π/x = 3π, 30π, 300π are multiples of π, so it also gives only 0s.
parts.n: LIM-1.C.3, LIM-1.C.4 (topic 1.3); skill 2.B. Thinking: choose inputs that test the claim instead of inputs that repeat the table's accident. Trap: (A), 'closer to 0' mistaken for 'more convincing'.

parts.q:
Suppose the student's function were instead g(x) = x·sin(π/x) for x ≠ 0. Which of the following is true about $\lim_{x \to 0} g(x)$?
(A) It does not exist, because the factor sin(π/x) keeps oscillating between −1 and 1 as x → 0.
(B) It is 0, by the product property of limits, because lim x = 0 and lim sin(π/x) = 0 by the table.
(C) It is 0, because −|x| ≤ x·sin(π/x) ≤ |x| for x ≠ 0 and both bounds approach 0.
(D) It is π, because x·sin(π/x) = π·sin(π/x)/(π/x), and sin(u)/u approaches 1.
parts.a: (C). Since −1 ≤ sin(π/x) ≤ 1, multiplying by |x| gives −|x| ≤ x·sin(π/x) ≤ |x| for every x ≠ 0. Both bounds approach 0 as x → 0, so by the Squeeze Theorem lim g(x) = 0. The oscillation is still there, but the factor x shrinks it to nothing. (A) ignores the shrinking factor x: the oscillation of sin(π/x) does not matter once it is multiplied by something that goes to 0. (B) reaches 0 by the product property, but that property needs both limits to exist, and lim sin(π/x) does not exist (question 3). (D) uses sin(u)/u → 1, which holds as u → 0; here u = π/x → ±∞ as x → 0, and sin(u)/u → 0. (The value π is the limit of x·sin(π/x) as x → ∞, not as x → 0.)
parts.n: LIM-1.E.2 (topic 1.8), with LIM-1.D.2; skill 3.C. Thinking: see that bounding the oscillating factor and letting x shrink it gives a squeeze. Trap: (B), the product property used when one of the limits does not exist.

mc.stem:
Questions 6-7 refer to the following.

A function g is defined for all real numbers and satisfies the inequality |g(x) − 3| ≤ (x − 2)² for all x. In words, the distance between g(x) and 3 is never more than (x − 2)². No other information about g is given.

parts.q:
Which of the following must be true?
I. $\lim_{x \to 2} g(x) = 3$
II. g is continuous at x = 2.
III. $\lim_{x \to 2} \frac{g(x) - 3}{x - 2} = 0$
(A) I only
(B) I and II only
(C) I and III only
(D) I, II, and III
parts.a: (D). Rewrite the inequality as 3 − (x − 2)² ≤ g(x) ≤ 3 + (x − 2)². I: both bounds approach 3 as x → 2, so by the Squeeze Theorem lim g(x) = 3. II: at x = 2 the inequality reads |g(2) − 3| ≤ 0, so g(2) = 3, which equals the limit; g is continuous at 2. III: for x ≠ 2, divide by |x − 2| to get |(g(x) − 3)/(x − 2)| ≤ |x − 2|, so −|x − 2| ≤ (g(x) − 3)/(x − 2) ≤ |x − 2|; both bounds approach 0, and the Squeeze Theorem gives the limit 0. (A) uses the squeeze for the limit but overlooks that the inequality also holds at x = 2 itself and pins down g(2). (B) stops before III; the same inequality, divided by |x − 2|, squeezes the quotient. (C) accepts III but not II, again missing that the inequality at x = 2 forces g(2) = 3.
parts.n: LIM-1.E.2 (topic 1.8), LIM-2.A.2 (topic 1.11); skill 3.C. Thinking: turn an absolute-value bound into a two-sided squeeze, and apply it to g(2) and to a quotient as well as to the limit. Trap: (A), the squeeze used for the limit but not for the value at 2.

parts.q:
A student writes: "From the inequality, 3 − (x − 2)² ≤ g(x) ≤ 3 + (x − 2)². As x → 4, the lower bound approaches −1 and the upper bound approaches 7. So by the Squeeze Theorem, $\lim_{x \to 4} g(x)$ exists and lies between −1 and 7." Which of the following best evaluates the student's argument?
(A) It is correct: the Squeeze Theorem traps the limit of g between the limits of the lower and upper bounds.
(B) It fails: the Squeeze Theorem needs both bounds to have the same limit, so g need not have a limit at 4.
(C) It fails, and in fact $\lim_{x \to 4} g(x)$ cannot exist, because the two bounds approach different values.
(D) It fails: the inequality describes g only near x = 2, so it gives no information at all about g near x = 4.
parts.a: (B). The Squeeze Theorem concludes that a limit exists only when the lower and upper bounds approach the same number; then the function caught between them has that limit too. Here the bounds approach −1 and 7, so the theorem says nothing about whether lim g(x) exists at x = 4. For example, g could equal 3 + (x − 2)² for x ≤ 4 and 3 − (x − 2)² for x > 4; it satisfies the inequality and has a jump at x = 4. (A) invents a version of the theorem: bounds with different limits cannot force a limit to exist. (C) overcorrects: g could have a limit at 4 (g(x) = 3 for all x satisfies the inequality); the bounds just do not decide it. (D) is false: the inequality holds for all x, so near x = 4 it does bound g between about −1 and 7; it just cannot produce a limit there.
parts.n: LIM-1.E.2 (topic 1.8); skill 3.C. Thinking: check the hypothesis of the Squeeze Theorem (bounds with a common limit) before using its conclusion. Trap: (C), 'the theorem does not apply' turned into 'the limit does not exist'.

mc.stem:
Questions 8-9 refer to the following.

A student is asked to find $\lim_{x \to 5} f(x)$ for $f(x) = \frac{\sqrt{x+4} - 3}{x^{2} - 25}$ and to decide whether f is continuous at x = 5. The student's work is shown.
Line 1: Substituting x = 5 gives 0/0, so more work is needed.
Line 2: $f(x) = \frac{(\sqrt{x+4} - 3)(\sqrt{x+4} + 3)}{(x^{2} - 25)(\sqrt{x+4} + 3)} = \frac{x - 5}{(x - 5)(x + 5)(\sqrt{x+4} + 3)}$
Line 3: $= \frac{1}{(x + 5)(\sqrt{x+4} + 3)}$
Line 4: So $\lim_{x \to 5} f(x) = \frac{1}{(10)(6)} = \frac{1}{60}$.
Line 5: The expression in Line 3 is defined at x = 5, so f(5) = 1/60 and f is continuous at x = 5.

parts.q:
Which of the following identifies the first error in the student's work?
(A) Line 5: the limit is 1/60, but f(5) is still undefined, so f is not continuous at x = 5.
(B) Line 1: a result of 0/0 on substitution means the limit does not exist, so the work should stop.
(C) Line 3: the factor x − 5 cannot be canceled, because x − 5 is equal to 0 when x = 5.
(D) Line 2: multiplying by (√(x + 4) + 3)/(√(x + 4) + 3) changes the value of the expression.
parts.a: (A). Lines 1 to 4 are correct. 0/0 signals that algebra is needed; multiplying by a form of 1 does not change the value; and canceling x − 5 is valid because a limit as x → 5 uses only x ≠ 5. So the limit is 1/60. But the simplified expression equals f(x) only for x ≠ 5: the original formula still gives 0/0 at x = 5, so f(5) does not exist, and f has a removable discontinuity there. Continuity needs f(5) to exist and equal the limit. (B) treats 0/0 as an answer; it is an indeterminate form that tells you to rewrite the expression. (C) forgets that the limit never uses x = 5 itself, so dividing out x − 5 (which is nonzero for x ≠ 5) is allowed. (D) misses that (√(x + 4) + 3)/(√(x + 4) + 3) equals 1 for every x in the domain.
parts.n: LIM-1.E.1 (topic 1.6), LIM-2.A.1, LIM-2.A.2 (topics 1.10, 1.11); skill 3.G. Thinking: separate what the simplified expression tells you about the limit from what it tells you about f(5). Trap: (C), refusing to cancel.

parts.q:
Suppose the numerator were $\sqrt{x+4} - 2$ instead, so the student must find $\lim_{x \to 5} \frac{\sqrt{x+4} - 2}{x^{2} - 25}$. Which of the following is correct?
(A) The limit is 1/50, from Lines 2 to 4 with each 3 replaced by 2.
(B) The limit is +∞, because the numerator approaches 1 and the denominator approaches 0.
(C) The limit does not exist, because substituting x = 5 again gives 0/0.
(D) The limit does not exist: the quotient → −∞ as x → 5⁻ and → +∞ as x → 5⁺.
parts.a: (D). Substitution now gives (3 − 2)/0 = 1/0, not 0/0, so no algebra is needed and none will help: the numerator approaches 1 while the denominator approaches 0. For 4 < x < 5, x² − 25 < 0, so the quotient is a positive number over a small negative number and → −∞; for x > 5 the denominator is positive and the quotient → +∞. The one-sided limits disagree, so the two-sided limit does not exist (x = 5 is a vertical asymptote). (A) repeats the conjugate steps by habit; with 2 in place of 3 the numerator becomes x, and no factor x − 5 appears to cancel. (B) finds the size of the blow-up but not its sign from the left, where the denominator is negative. (C) has the right verdict for the wrong reason: the form here is 1/0, and a 0/0 form alone would not mean the limit fails to exist.
parts.n: LIM-1.E.1 (topic 1.7), LIM-2.D.1, LIM-2.D.2; skill 1.C. Thinking: classify the form (0/0 or nonzero/0) before choosing a procedure, then find the sign of the denominator on each side. Trap: (A), applying the conjugate procedure by reflex.

mc.stem:
Questions 10-11 refer to the following.

Let f be the function defined by
$f(x) = \frac{x^{2} + ax + b}{x - 3}$ for x ≠ 3, and f(3) = 7,
where a and b are constants. Different choices of a and b give f different kinds of behavior at x = 3.

parts.q:
For which values of a and b is f continuous at x = 3?
(A) a = 4 and b = −21
(B) a = 1 and b = 12
(C) a = 1 and b = −12
(D) No values of a and b work, because the denominator is 0 at x = 3.
parts.a: (C). As x → 3 the denominator approaches 0, so the limit can be finite only if the numerator also approaches 0: 9 + 3a + b = 0. Then x − 3 is a factor, x² + ax + b = (x − 3)(x + c), and f(x) = x + c for x ≠ 3, so lim f(x) = 3 + c. Continuity needs 3 + c = f(3) = 7, so c = 4 and x² + ax + b = (x − 3)(x + 4) = x² + x − 12: a = 1, b = −12. (A) sets c = 7, the value of f(3), forgetting that the limit is 3 + c: (x − 3)(x + 7) = x² + 4x − 21 gives a limit of 10. (B) has a sign slip in b: x² + x + 12 equals 24 at x = 3, so f would have a vertical asymptote there. (D) forgets that a zero denominator can be canceled by a zero numerator; a removable gap can be filled.
parts.n: LIM-2.C.1, LIM-2.C.2 (topic 1.13), LIM-1.E.1; skill 1.E. Thinking: reason that a finite limit over a vanishing denominator forces a vanishing numerator, then match the limit to f(3). Trap: (A), setting the leftover factor's constant equal to f(3).

parts.q:
Suppose instead that a = 1 and b = −10, with f(3) = 7 as before. Which of the following best describes the behavior of f at x = 3?
(A) A removable discontinuity, since f(3) = 7 is defined and only the formula near x = 3 changes.
(B) An infinite discontinuity: f(x) → −∞ as x → 3⁻ and f(x) → +∞ as x → 3⁺.
(C) A jump discontinuity, since the one-sided limits of f at x = 3 are two different numbers.
(D) No discontinuity, since f(3) = 7 is defined and x² + x − 10 is a polynomial.
parts.a: (B). Now the numerator approaches 9 + 3 − 10 = 2 while the denominator x − 3 approaches 0. For x slightly less than 3, x − 3 < 0, so f(x) is about 2 divided by a small negative number and → −∞; for x slightly more than 3, f(x) → +∞. The graph has a vertical asymptote at x = 3, an infinite discontinuity; the value f(3) = 7 cannot repair it. (A) assumes any discontinuity with a defined f(3) is removable; removable requires the limit to exist, and here f is unbounded. (C) calls it a jump, but a jump needs finite one-sided limits; these are infinite. (D) checks only that f(3) is defined and that the numerator is continuous, ignoring the limit.
parts.n: LIM-2.A.1 (topic 1.10), LIM-2.D.2; skill 3.B. Thinking: evaluate the numerator's limit to tell a removable gap from an asymptote, then read the sign on each side. Trap: (A), 'f(3) is defined, so the discontinuity is removable'.

parts.q:
Let $f(x) = \frac{\sin x}{x^{2} - \pi x}$. A student says, "The denominator x² − πx = x(x − π) is 0 at x = 0 and at x = π, so the graph of f has vertical asymptotes at x = 0 and at x = π." Which of the following best evaluates the student's claim?
(A) Incorrect: both are removable discontinuities, since f approaches −1/π at x = 0 and at x = π.
(B) Correct: wherever the denominator of a quotient is 0, the graph of the quotient has a vertical asymptote.
(C) Partly correct: x = 0 is removable because sin x/x → 1 there, but x = π is a vertical asymptote.
(D) Incorrect: both discontinuities are removable, but the limits differ: −1/π at x = 0 and 1/π at x = π.
parts.a: (A). At x = 0: f(x) = (sin x/x)·1/(x − π) → (1)(−1/π) = −1/π. At x = π: let u = x − π; then sin x = sin(u + π) = −sin u, and f(x) = −sin u/(u(u + π)) = −(sin u/u)·1/(u + π) → −(1)(1/π) = −1/π. Both limits are finite, so f has removable discontinuities (holes) at x = 0 and x = π and no vertical asymptote. (B) forgets that the numerator is also 0 at both points; a 0/0 form can have a finite limit. (C) handles x = 0 with the known limit but assumes the other zero is an asymptote; sin x also vanishes at π, and the quotient has a finite limit there. (D) treats sin x/(x − π) like sin x/x and gets +1; near π the sine is positive on the left and negative on the right while x − π has the opposite signs, so the quotient approaches −1.
parts.n: LIM-2.D.1, LIM-2.D.2 (topic 1.14), LIM-1.E.1; skill 3.D. Thinking: before calling a zero of a denominator an asymptote, check the numerator there and compute the limit. Trap: (C), trusting sin x/x → 1 at 0 but not reworking the limit at π.

mc.stem:
Questions 13-14 refer to the following.

A parking garage charges 4 dollars for the first hour or any part of it, and 3 dollars for each additional hour or part of an hour, but never more than 20 dollars for a stay of up to 24 hours. Let C(t) be the charge, in dollars, for a stay of t hours, where 0 < t ≤ 24. For example, C(1) = 4, C(1.2) = 7 and C(2) = 7.

parts.q:
What is the value of $\lim_{t \to 6^{+}} C(t) - \lim_{t \to 6^{-}} C(t)$, and what does it tell a driver?
(A) 3; staying just past 6 hours adds another 3 dollars for the seventh hour.
(B) 0; because of the 20-dollar maximum, the charge does not change at t = 6.
(C) It has no value, because the two-sided limit $\lim_{t \to 6} C(t)$ does not exist.
(D) 1; past 6 hours the 20-dollar cap applies, so the charge rises from 19 to 20.
parts.a: (D). For 5 < t ≤ 6 the charge is 4 + 3(5) = 19 dollars, so the limit from the left at t = 6 is 19. For t just past 6 a seventh hour would bring the charge to 22 dollars, but the maximum caps it at 20 dollars, so the limit from the right is 20. The difference, 20 − 19 = 1, is the extra cost of staying just past 6 hours. (A) applies the 3-dollar rule without the cap. (B) sees the cap but applies it too early; the charge first reaches 20 dollars only after 6 hours. (C) confuses the two-sided limit, which does not exist, with the one-sided limits, which both exist and can be subtracted.
parts.n: LIM-1.B.1 (topic 1.2), LIM-1.C.1; skill 3.F. Thinking: model the charge on each side of t = 6 and read the one-sided limits in context. Trap: (A), the 3-dollar pattern continued past the cap.

parts.q:
A driver argues, "C(2) = 7 and $\lim_{t \to 2^{-}} C(t) = 7$, so C is continuous at t = 2. That means staying a few seconds past the 2-hour mark costs nothing extra." Which of the following best evaluates the driver's argument?
(A) It is wrong: $\lim_{t \to 2^{+}} C(t) = 10$, so C jumps at t = 2 and a few extra seconds cost 3 dollars.
(B) It is right: C(2) exists and equals the limit from the left, and that is all continuity at t = 2 requires.
(C) It is wrong: C(2) is undefined, since a stay of exactly 2 hours could be billed as either 2 or 3 hours.
(D) It is right about the cost, since a few seconds is less than an hour, but C is not continuous at t = 2.
parts.a: (A). Continuity at t = 2 needs the two-sided limit to exist and equal C(2). From the left the charge is 7 dollars, but for any stay a little longer than 2 hours the third hour has started, so the charge is 10 dollars: lim C(t) as t → 2⁺ is 10. The one-sided limits differ, the limit does not exist, and C has a jump at t = 2, which is exactly the extra 3 dollars for staying a few seconds more. (B) checks only one side; agreement from the left makes C continuous from the left, not continuous. (C) contradicts the rule, which bills a stay of exactly 2 hours as two hours: C(2) = 7 is given. (D) gets the continuity right but the cost wrong: the rule charges for any part of an hour.
parts.n: LIM-2.A.2 (topic 1.11), LIM-2.A.1; skill 3.C. Thinking: check both one-sided limits against the function value, and read the jump as a cost. Trap: (B), left-hand agreement mistaken for continuity.

parts.q:
The function g is continuous on the closed interval [0, 4]. Selected values of g are given in the table.
x · 0 · 1 · 2 · 3 · 4
g(x) · 4 · 1 · 3 · −2 · 0
Which of the following must be true?
I. The equation g(x) = 2 has at least three solutions in the open interval (0, 4).
II. The equation g(x) = 0 has at least two solutions in the closed interval [0, 4].
III. The equation g(x) = −3 has no solution in the closed interval [0, 4].
(A) I only
(B) I and II only
(C) I and III only
(D) I, II, and III
parts.a: (B). I: g is continuous, and 2 lies between g(0) = 4 and g(1) = 1, between g(1) = 1 and g(2) = 3, and between g(2) = 3 and g(3) = −2, so the Intermediate Value Theorem gives a solution in each of (0, 1), (1, 2) and (2, 3): at least three. II: 0 lies between g(2) = 3 and g(3) = −2, giving a solution in (2, 3), and g(4) = 0 is a second solution. III need not be true: the table gives only five values, and g can dip below −3 between x = 2 and x = 4 without contradicting any of them. (A) misses the solution at x = 4 itself; a value in the table can be a solution. (C) reads the table's smallest value as the least value of g. (D) makes the same mistake as (C); the IVT guarantees values, but never rules one out.
parts.n: FUN-1.A.1 (topic 1.16); skill 3.E. Thinking: apply the IVT interval by interval, count endpoints that already solve the equation, and recognize what the theorem cannot rule out. Trap: (C), the table taken as the range of g.

parts.q:
The functions f and g are defined for all real numbers. Their one-sided limits at x = 2 are given in the table.
function · limit as x → 2⁻ · limit as x → 2⁺
f · 3 · 1
g · −1 · 1
A student says, "Neither $\lim_{x \to 2} f(x)$ nor $\lim_{x \to 2} g(x)$ exists, so no limit at x = 2 built from f and g can exist." Which of the following limits exist?
I. $\lim_{x \to 2} [f(x) + g(x)]$
II. $\lim_{x \to 2} f(x)g(x)$
III. $\lim_{x \to 2} f(x)[g(x) + 2]$
(A) None of them, as the student says
(B) I only
(C) I and III only
(D) I, II, and III
parts.a: (C). Work one side at a time. I: from the left 3 + (−1) = 2, from the right 1 + 1 = 2; the one-sided limits agree, so the limit exists and equals 2. II: from the left 3(−1) = −3, from the right 1(1) = 1; they differ, so the limit does not exist. III: from the left 3(−1 + 2) = 3, from the right 1(1 + 2) = 3; the limit exists and equals 3. The limit properties need each piece's limit to exist, but when they do not, one-sided limits can still settle the question. (A) accepts the student's claim; the jumps in f and g can cancel. (B) finds the sum but assumes a product of two jumps cannot have a limit; III shows it can. (D) includes II, but its one-sided limits are −3 and 1.
parts.n: LIM-1.D.1, LIM-1.D.2 (topic 1.5); skill 3.G. Thinking: when the limit properties do not apply, compute each one-sided limit of the whole expression. Trap: (A), 'the pieces have no limit, so the combination has none'.

mc.stem:
Questions 17-18 refer to the following.

Let f(x) = xˣ for x > 0. A student wants the instantaneous rate of change of f at x = 2 but knows no rule for differentiating a function like this one, so the student uses a calculator to find average rates of change of f over intervals that have x = 2 as an endpoint.

parts.q:
Which of the following is closest to the instantaneous rate of change of f at x = 2?
(A) 7.496
(B) 6.773
(C) 4.000
(D) 3.000
parts.a: (B). Average rates of change over [2, 2 + h] for h = 0.1, 0.01, 0.001 are 7.496, 6.840, 6.779, and over [2 − h, 2] they are 6.144, 6.706, 6.766. The two sequences close in from above and below on the same number, about 6.773 (the average over [1.999, 2.001] is 6.7726). (A) is the average rate over [2, 2.1]; that interval is too wide, and the averages keep changing a great deal as h shrinks. (C) is f(2) = 4, the value of the function, not its rate of change (it is also what a misapplied power rule, x·xˣ⁻¹, gives). (D) is the average rate over [1, 2], (4 − 1)/1 = 3, far too coarse an interval.
parts.n: CHA-1.A.3 (topic 1.1), LIM-1.C.5; skill 1.E. Thinking: generate average rates over shrinking intervals on both sides and read off the common value they approach. Trap: (A), stopping at the first small-looking interval.

parts.q:
The student's first attempt used the interval [2, 2.5], giving an average rate of change of (f(2.5) − f(2))/0.5 ≈ 11.764. Which of the following best describes this estimate?
(A) It is too large: as h shrinks, the average rates over [2, 2 + h] decrease toward about 6.773.
(B) It is too small: the average rates over [2, 2 + h] increase toward the instantaneous rate as the interval shrinks.
(C) It is too large, because f(2.5) is greater than f(2), and an average rate of an increasing function is always an overestimate.
(D) It cannot be compared, because an average rate over an interval and a rate at an instant measure different things.
parts.a: (A). The average rates over [2, 2 + h] are 11.764 for h = 0.5, 7.496 for h = 0.1, 6.840 for h = 0.01 and 6.779 for h = 0.001: they decrease toward the instantaneous rate, about 6.773. So the interval [2, 2.5] gives an estimate that is far too large; f is getting steeper to the right of 2, and the wide interval averages in those steeper slopes. (B) has the direction backwards; the calculator values decrease as h shrinks. (C) reaches the right verdict for a wrong reason: an increasing function can have average rates that are too small (from the left of 2 the averages 6.144, 6.706, 6.766 are all too small). (D) misses the point of topic 1.1: the instantaneous rate is defined as the limit of average rates, so the two can be compared directly.
parts.n: CHA-1.A.1, CHA-1.A.3 (topic 1.1); skill 1.F. Thinking: use the trend of the calculator's average rates to decide whether a coarse estimate is high or low. Trap: (C), increasing mistaken for 'average rates overestimate'.

parts.q:
Let f be the function defined by $f(x) = e^{kx}$ for x ≤ 1 and f(x) = 3 − kx for x > 1, where k is a constant. For what value of k is f continuous at x = 1?
(A) 1.099
(B) 2.208
(C) 1.505
(D) 0.792
parts.a: (D). Both pieces are continuous, so only x = 1 matters. There f(1) and the limit from the left are $e^{k}$, and the limit from the right is 3 − k. Continuity needs $e^{k} = 3 - k$, an equation with no algebraic solution: graph y = eˣ and y = 3 − x (or find the zero of eˣ + x − 3) to get k ≈ 0.792. (A) is ln 3, from solving $e^{k} = 3$, which drops the −k. (B) is the y-coordinate of the intersection point, $e^{0.792}$ ≈ 2.208, reported instead of its x-coordinate. (C) solves $e^{k} = 3 + k$, a sign slip in the right-hand piece.
parts.n: LIM-2.C.2 (topic 1.13), LIM-2.B.2; skill 1.E. Thinking: match the two one-sided limits at the boundary and solve the resulting equation with a calculator. Trap: (B), reading the wrong coordinate of the intersection.

parts.q:
Let $f(x) = \frac{x}{e^{x} - 3x}$. Which of the following statements about the vertical asymptotes of the graph of f, and the behavior of f near them, is true?
(A) It has no vertical asymptote, because eˣ > 3x for every real number x.
(B) It has vertical asymptotes at x ≈ 0.619 and x ≈ 1.512, and f(x) → −∞ as x → 1.512⁺.
(C) It has vertical asymptotes at x ≈ 0.619 and x ≈ 1.512, and f(x) → +∞ as x → 1.512⁺.
(D) It has vertical asymptotes at x ≈ 0.619 and x ≈ 1.512, and f(x) → +∞ as x → 0.619⁺.
parts.a: (C). A calculator shows eˣ − 3x = 0 at x ≈ 0.619 and x ≈ 1.512, where the numerator x is not 0, so both are vertical asymptotes. The denominator is negative between the two zeros (at x = 1 it is e − 3 < 0) and positive outside them. Just to the right of 1.512 the numerator is about 1.5 and the denominator is a small positive number, so f(x) → +∞. (A) assumes an exponential is always bigger than a linear function; eˣ − 3x is negative at x = 1. (B) gets the asymptotes but the wrong sign: to the right of the larger zero the denominator is positive. (D) gets the sign wrong at the smaller zero: just to the right of 0.619 the denominator is negative, so f(x) → −∞.
parts.n: LIM-2.D.1, LIM-2.D.2 (topic 1.14); skill 3.D. Thinking: locate the zeros of the denominator with a calculator, confirm the numerator is not zero there, and find the sign of the denominator on each side. Trap: (B), a sign slip on the side of the asymptote.

parts.q:
A student compares x¹⁰ and 2ˣ for large x and makes the table below.
x · x¹⁰ · 2ˣ
10 · 1.0000 × 10¹⁰ · 1.0240 × 10³
30 · 5.9049 × 10¹⁴ · 1.0737 × 10⁹
50 · 9.7656 × 10¹⁶ · 1.1259 × 10¹⁵
Because x¹⁰ is larger at every x in the table, the student concludes that $\lim_{x \to \infty} \frac{x^{10}}{2^{x}} = \infty$. Which of the following best evaluates the student's conclusion?
(A) It is correct: at every x in the table, x¹⁰ is far larger than 2ˣ, so the ratio grows without bound.
(B) It is wrong: the limit is 1, because x¹⁰ and 2ˣ both grow without bound as x → ∞.
(C) It is wrong: 2ˣ passes x¹⁰ at x ≈ 58.770, but x¹⁰ passes 2ˣ again later, so the limit does not exist.
(D) It is wrong: 2ˣ passes x¹⁰ at x ≈ 58.770 and stays larger after that, so the limit is 0.
parts.a: (D). Solving 2ˣ = x¹⁰ on a calculator (for instance, the zero of x ln 2 − 10 ln x) gives x ≈ 58.770; at x = 60 the ratio x¹⁰/2ˣ is already about 0.52. An exponential function with base greater than 1 eventually dominates every power function, so the ratio approaches 0 as x → ∞. The table stopped too soon. (A) trusts a table that does not reach the part of the domain that decides end behavior; the ratio is already falling (about 9.8 million at x = 10, about 550,000 at x = 30, about 87 at x = 50). (B) treats ∞/∞ as 1; comparing how fast the two grow is the whole question. (C) finds the crossing but imagines the power function coming back; once 2ˣ passes x¹⁰ it stays ahead, because x¹⁰/2ˣ decreases for x > 10/ln 2 ≈ 14.4.
parts.n: LIM-2.D.4, LIM-2.D.5 (topic 1.15); skill 3.G. Thinking: test a pattern from a table against what limits say about relative growth, and use the calculator to find where the pattern breaks. Trap: (A), a table that stops before the crossing.

parts.q:
Let $f(x) = \frac{\ln(4 - x^{2})}{x - \cos x}$. Which of the following is the set of all x at which f is continuous?
(A) −2 < x < 0.739 and 0.739 < x < 2
(B) −2 < x < 2
(C) x < 0.739 and x > 0.739
(D) −2 < x < 1.000 and 1.000 < x < 2
parts.a: (A). Logarithmic, polynomial and trigonometric functions are continuous on their domains, so f is continuous wherever it is defined. ln(4 − x²) needs 4 − x² > 0, that is −2 < x < 2. The denominator x − cos x is 0 where x = cos x; a calculator (in radian mode) gives x ≈ 0.739, the only solution, since x − cos x is increasing. So f is continuous on −2 < x < 0.739 and on 0.739 < x < 2. (B) forgets the zero of the denominator. (C) forgets that the logarithm is undefined for |x| ≥ 2. (D) solves x = cos x with the calculator in degree mode, where cos(1°) ≈ 0.99985.
parts.n: LIM-2.B.1, LIM-2.B.2 (topic 1.12); skill 1.E. Thinking: combine the domain of each piece with the zero of the denominator, found with a calculator. Trap: (C), overlooking the logarithm's domain.

parts.q:
The depth of the water at a harbor entrance, in feet, is modeled by D(t) = 3 + 2 sin t + 0.3t for 0 ≤ t ≤ 8, where t is measured in hours. A student says, "D is continuous, D(0) = 3 and D(8) ≈ 7.379, so by the Intermediate Value Theorem the depth is 5 feet at exactly one time between t = 0 and t = 8." Which of the following best evaluates the student's statement?
(A) It is correct: the IVT guarantees exactly one such time, and a calculator shows that it is t ≈ 1.012.
(B) It is wrong: the IVT guarantees at least one such time; D(t) = 5 at t ≈ 1.012, 2.458 and 6.333.
(C) It is wrong: the IVT does not apply because D is not increasing on [0, 8], so D may never equal 5.
(D) It is wrong: the IVT guarantees at least one such time; in fact D(t) = 5 only at t ≈ 1.012 and 6.333.
parts.a: (B). The IVT applies (D is continuous on [0, 8] and 5 is between 3 and 7.379) and guarantees at least one time with D(t) = 5, never exactly one. Graphing y = D(t) and y = 5 on [0, 8] shows three intersections: t ≈ 1.012 (rising), 2.458 (falling after a high tide) and 6.333 (rising again). (A) reads 'at least one' as 'exactly one' and stops at the first intersection. (C) adds a hypothesis the theorem does not have: the IVT needs continuity, not monotonicity. (D) misses the crossing at t ≈ 2.458, just after the local maximum near t = 1.7; a window that is too coarse can hide it.
parts.n: FUN-1.A.1 (topic 1.16); skill 3.E. Thinking: separate what the IVT guarantees (existence) from what the graph shows (how many), and check the theorem's actual hypotheses. Trap: (A), 'exactly one'.

parts.q:
Let $f(x) = \frac{2^{x} - 1}{x}$ for x ≠ 0, and let f(0) = 0.693. A student computes f(0.001) and f(−0.001) on a calculator, sees that both round to 0.693, and concludes that $\lim_{x \to 0} f(x) = 0.693 = f(0)$, so f is continuous at x = 0. Which of the following best evaluates the student's conclusion?
(A) It is correct: the values of f on both sides of 0 round to 0.693, which is the value of f(0).
(B) It is wrong: f(0.001) and f(−0.001) are different, so the one-sided limits differ and f has a jump at 0.
(C) It is wrong: f(0.0001) ≈ 0.693171 and f(−0.0001) ≈ 0.693123 trap the limit near 0.69315, not 0.693.
(D) It is wrong: at x = 0 the formula gives 0/0, so the limit does not exist and f cannot be continuous there.
parts.a: (C). Closer to 0 the calculator gives f(−0.0001) ≈ 0.693123 and f(0.0001) ≈ 0.693171; f increases through 0, so the limit lies between these, near 0.69315 (it is ln 2 ≈ 0.693147). The number 0.693 is outside that interval, so lim f(x) ≠ f(0) and f is not continuous at 0 (a removable discontinuity; defining f(0) = ln 2 would repair it). Continuity needs exact equality, and agreement to three decimal places is not equality. (A) confuses a rounded value with the exact limit. (B) mistakes two nearby values of a continuous-looking function for two different one-sided limits; both sequences approach the same number. (D) treats 0/0 as meaning no limit; this 0/0 form has a limit, it just is not 0.693.
parts.n: LIM-2.A.2 (topic 1.11), LIM-1.C.5; skill 3.G. Thinking: use calculator values to trap the limit and compare it with f(0) exactly, not to three decimal places. Trap: (A), rounding taken as equality.

fr.title: A meal in the oven: when it is safe, how fast it warms, and the switch-off
fr.stem:
A frozen meal is placed in a hot oven at time t = 0. For 0 ≤ t ≤ 25, the temperature of the meal, in degrees Celsius, is modeled by $T(t) = 180 - 198e^{-0.07t}$, where t is measured in minutes. At t = 25 the meal is taken out of the oven, and for t > 25 its temperature is modeled by $T(t) = 22 + Be^{-0.05(t - 25)}$, where B is a constant.
A graphing calculator is allowed. Give decimal answers to three decimal places.

parts.q: The meal is safe to eat once its temperature reaches 74 degrees Celsius. Explain why there must be a time t in the interval 0 < t < 25 at which T(t) = 74. Then find that time.
parts.a: T is continuous on [0, 25], because it is built from an exponential function. T(0) = 180 − 198 = −18 and T(25) = 180 − 198e^(−1.75) ≈ 145.593, and −18 < 74 < 145.593 (1 point). So by the Intermediate Value Theorem there is a time c in (0, 25) with T(c) = 74 (1 point). Solving 180 − 198e^(−0.07t) = 74 on the calculator gives t ≈ 8.926 minutes (1 point).
parts.n: 'T starts cold and ends hot, so it must pass 74' with no mention of continuity, or with no values of T(0) and T(25), earns no theorem point. Naming the IVT for a function that is not stated to be continuous earns at most one of the first two points.

parts.q: Use average rates of change of T over the intervals [10, 10 + h] for h = 0.1, h = 0.01 and h = 0.001 to estimate the instantaneous rate of change of T at t = 10. Show the averages, and give your estimate with units.
parts.a: The averages (T(10 + h) − T(10))/h are 6.859, 6.880 and 6.882 for h = 0.1, 0.01 and 0.001 (1 point). They settle near 6.88, so the temperature is rising at about 6.88 degrees Celsius per minute at t = 10 (1 point). (Averages over [10 − h, 10], 6.907, 6.885 and 6.883, approach the same value from above.)
parts.n: An average rate over one wide interval, such as (T(12) − T(10))/2, earns nothing for the estimate. A value with no units, or with units of degrees instead of degrees per minute, loses the second point. The value T(10) ≈ 81.676 is a temperature, not a rate.

parts.q: A student estimates the instantaneous rate of change of T at t = 10 with the average rate of change of T over [10, 12]. Is the student's estimate an overestimate or an underestimate? Explain your reasoning.
parts.a: An underestimate (1 point). The average over [10, 12] is (T(12) − T(10))/2 ≈ (94.521 − 81.676)/2 ≈ 6.423, and the averages over [10, 10 + h] increase as h shrinks: 6.423 for h = 2, 6.647 for h = 1, 6.859 for h = 0.1, toward about 6.88. So a wide interval to the right gives a value that is too small. In context, the meal warms more slowly as its temperature approaches the oven's, so the slower minutes after t = 10 pull the average down (1 point).
parts.n: 'Overestimate, because T is increasing' earns nothing: an increasing function can have averages that are too small. 'Underestimate' with no comparison of values or of how the rate changes earns only the first point.

parts.q: Find the value of B for which T is continuous at t = 25. A student then says, "With this value of B, T is continuous at t = 25, so the meal's temperature is changing at the same rate just before and just after t = 25." Is the student correct? Explain your reasoning.
parts.a: Continuity at 25 needs 22 + B = T(25) = 180 − 198e^(−1.75), so B ≈ 123.593 (1 point). The student is not correct (1 point): the average rate over [24.99, 25] is about 2.409 degrees per minute (still warming), and over [25, 25.01] it is about −6.178 degrees per minute (cooling). Continuity means the temperature has no jump at t = 25; it says nothing about the rate being the same on both sides.
parts.n: B = 145.593 (setting B equal to T(25) and forgetting the 22) earns nothing for the first point. Agreeing with the student, or disagreeing with no evidence about the rates on the two sides, earns nothing for the second.

fr.title: Two breaks in a function: classifying, repairing and still finding a zero
fr.stem:
The function f is defined for all real numbers and is continuous at every x except x = 2 and x = 4. The following facts about f are known.
• $\lim_{x \to 2^{-}} f(x) = 3$, $\lim_{x \to 2^{+}} f(x) = -1$, and f(2) = 3.
• $\lim_{x \to 4} f(x) = 5$ and f(4) = 1.
• f(3) = 2.
A calculator is not allowed.

parts.q: Classify the discontinuity of f at x = 2 and the discontinuity of f at x = 4, and justify each classification using limits. At which of the two points could f be made continuous by changing a single function value?
parts.a: At x = 2, a jump discontinuity: both one-sided limits exist but 3 ≠ −1, so $\lim_{x \to 2} f(x)$ does not exist (1 point). At x = 4, a removable discontinuity: $\lim_{x \to 4} f(x) = 5$ exists but does not equal f(4) = 1. Redefining f(4) = 5 would make f continuous at 4; no value of f(2) can help at 2, because there is no limit for it to equal (1 point).
parts.n: Calling x = 2 removable because f(2) = 3 matches the left-hand limit earns nothing. 'Jump' and 'removable' with no limits quoted earn nothing.

parts.q: Let g(x) = (x − 2)f(x). Is g continuous at x = 2? Justify your answer using the definition of continuity.
parts.a: Yes. g(2) = (0)f(2) = 0. From the left, g(x) → (0)(3) = 0; from the right, g(x) → (0)(−1) = 0, so $\lim_{x \to 2} g(x) = 0$ (1 point). Since the limit exists and equals g(2), g is continuous at x = 2, even though f is not (1 point).
parts.n: 'No, because f is not continuous at 2' earns nothing: the factor x − 2 closes the jump. Computing only g(2), or only one one-sided limit, earns at most the second point if the conclusion checks all three conditions.

parts.q: A student says, "f is not continuous on [2, 3], so the Intermediate Value Theorem cannot be used, and we cannot conclude that the equation f(x) = 0 has a solution in the open interval (2, 3)." Do you agree? Justify your answer.
parts.a: No (1 point). The IVT cannot be applied on [2, 3], but it can be applied on a smaller interval. Because $\lim_{x \to 2^{+}} f(x) = -1 < 0$, the values of f just to the right of 2 are close to −1, so there is a number b with 2 < b < 3 and f(b) < 0 (1 point). The only breaks in f are at 2 and 4, so f is continuous on [b, 3], and f(b) < 0 < 2 = f(3). By the Intermediate Value Theorem there is a c in (b, 3), and so in (2, 3), with f(c) = 0 (1 point).
parts.n: Agreeing with the student earns nothing. Applying the IVT on [2, 3] with f(2) = 3 and f(3) = 2 earns nothing: those values do not bracket 0, and f is not continuous there. Saying 'f goes from −1 to 2' without choosing a point b where f is actually negative loses the second point.

parts.q: Find $\lim_{x \to 2} \left[ f(x)^{2} - 2f(x) \right]$, or show that it does not exist.
parts.a: From the left, f(x) → 3, so the expression → 9 − 6 = 3; from the right, f(x) → −1, so it → 1 + 2 = 3 (1 point). The one-sided limits agree, so the limit exists and equals 3 (1 point).
parts.n: 'Does not exist, because lim f(x) does not exist' earns nothing; the limit properties do not apply, but the one-sided limits settle it. Substituting f(2) = 3 to get 3 with no one-sided limits earns nothing, even though the number is right.

fr.title: Asymptotes of a quotient with a sine term: a squeeze and a crossing
fr.stem:
Let f be the function defined by
$f(x) = \frac{6x^{2} + x\sin x}{2x^{2} - 8}$
for all x except x = 2 and x = −2.
A calculator is not allowed. You may use the fact that sin x > 0 for 0 < x < π.

parts.q: Show that the graph of f has vertical asymptotes at x = 2 and x = −2. Then find $\lim_{x \to 2^{-}} f(x)$ and $\lim_{x \to 2^{+}} f(x)$.
parts.a: At x = ±2 the denominator is 0, and the numerator is 24 ± 2 sin(±2) = 24 + 2 sin 2, which is positive (sin 2 > 0 since 0 < 2 < π), so the numerator does not approach 0 and f is unbounded near each point: both are vertical asymptotes (1 point). Near x = 2 the numerator is about 25.8 > 0; the denominator 2x² − 8 is negative for x slightly less than 2 and positive for x slightly more than 2. So $\lim_{x \to 2^{-}} f(x) = -\infty$ and $\lim_{x \to 2^{+}} f(x) = \infty$ (1 point).
parts.n: 'The denominator is 0, so there is an asymptote' with no check of the numerator earns nothing for the first point. Giving +∞ on both sides, or signs with no reason, loses the second point.

parts.q: Find $\lim_{x \to \infty} f(x)$. Justify your answer, using the Squeeze Theorem for the part of f that involves sin x.
parts.a: Write $f(x) = \frac{6x^{2}}{2x^{2} - 8} + \frac{x\sin x}{2x^{2} - 8}$. Dividing by x², the first term is $\frac{6}{2 - 8/x^{2}}$, which approaches 3 (1 point). For x > 2 the denominator is positive and −1 ≤ sin x ≤ 1, so $-\frac{x}{2x^{2} - 8} \le \frac{x\sin x}{2x^{2} - 8} \le \frac{x}{2x^{2} - 8}$ (1 point). Both bounds approach 0 as x → ∞, so by the Squeeze Theorem the second term approaches 0, and $\lim_{x \to \infty} f(x) = 3 + 0 = 3$ (1 point).
parts.n: Answering 3 'because the leading coefficients are 6 and 2' earns only the first point: sin x has no limit at infinity, so its term needs its own argument. Bounds written without noting that the denominator is positive, or a claim that x sin x/(2x² − 8) → 0 'because sin x is bounded' with no inequality, lose the second point.

parts.q: A student says, "Since y = 3 is a horizontal asymptote of the graph of f, the graph of f never crosses the line y = 3 for x > 2." Do you agree? Justify your answer.
parts.a: No (1 point). Subtracting, $f(x) - 3 = \frac{x\sin x + 24}{2x^{2} - 8}$, so for x > 2 the graph meets y = 3 exactly where x sin x = −24 (1 point). At x = 8π, sin x = 0, so f(8π) − 3 = 24/(2(8π)² − 8) > 0. At x = 19π/2, sin x = −1 and x sin x = −19π/2 < −24 (since 19π/2 > 28), so f(19π/2) − 3 < 0 (1 point). f is continuous on [8π, 19π/2], because its denominator is not 0 for x > 2, so by the Intermediate Value Theorem there is a c between 8π and 19π/2 with f(c) = 3 (1 point). The same argument works on every later interval [8π + 2πn, 19π/2 + 2πn], so the graph crosses its horizontal asymptote infinitely many times.
parts.n: Agreeing earns nothing: a horizontal asymptote describes end behavior, not a line the graph must avoid. Disagreeing with only a sketch or 'the sine makes it wiggle', with no values on each side of 3 and no IVT, earns only the first point. Applying the IVT without stating that f is continuous on the chosen interval loses the last point.

u4.intro: Multiple-choice questions 17-24 and free-response question 1 allow a graphing calculator; all other questions are no calculator.

mc.stem:
Questions 1-3 refer to the following.

A delivery truck makes a long trip. Let F(m) be the amount of fuel, in liters, in the truck's tank after it has driven m kilometers, for 0 ≤ m ≤ 300. The function F is twice differentiable, and F″(m) > 0 for 0 < m < 300. Selected values of F(m) and F′(m) are given in the table.
m (kilometers) · F(m) (liters) · F′(m) (liters per kilometer)
0 · 120 · −0.12
60 · 113.2 · −0.105
150 · 104.5 · −0.09
200 · 100.1 · −0.085
300 · 92 · −0.075

parts.q:
At the moment the truck has driven 150 kilometers, it is traveling at 90 kilometers per hour. At that moment, at what rate, in liters per hour, is the amount of fuel in the tank changing?
(A) −0.001
(B) −0.135
(C) −7.92
(D) −8.1
parts.a: (D). The table gives the rate with respect to distance; the question asks for the rate with respect to time. By the chain rule, dF/dt = (dF/dm)(dm/dt) = F′(150)·90 = (−0.09 liter per kilometer)(90 kilometers per hour) = −8.1 liters per hour. The kilometers cancel, which is the check that the product is the right one. (A) divides instead of multiplying, −0.09/90, which leaves liters per kilometer per (kilometer per hour), not liters per hour. (B) converts the speed to 1.5 kilometers per minute, so −0.135 is the rate in liters per minute, not per hour. (C) uses the average rate over [150, 200], (100.1 − 104.5)/50 = −0.088, instead of the instantaneous rate F′(150) that the table gives.
parts.n: CHA-3.C.1, CHA-3.D.1 (topic 4.3); skill 1.E. Thinking: turn a rate per kilometer into a rate per hour with the chain rule, letting the units show which operation is right. Trap: (A), dividing by the speed.

parts.q:
The driver notices that the values of F′(m) in the table increase from −0.12 to −0.075 and says, "F′ is increasing, so as the trip goes on the truck burns fuel faster and faster." Which of the following best evaluates the driver's statement?
(A) It is wrong: F′ rising toward 0 means each kilometer uses less fuel than the one before, so fuel use per kilometer is decreasing.
(B) It is right: F′ is the rate of fuel use, and a rate that increases means the fuel is being used up faster.
(C) It is wrong: F is decreasing, so F′ must also be decreasing, which means the values in the table cannot be correct.
(D) It is right: F″ > 0 means the graph of F is concave up, so F is decreasing more and more steeply as m grows.
parts.a: (A). F′(m) is the change in fuel per kilometer, and it is negative because fuel is used. The truck uses |F′(m)| liters per kilometer: 0.12 at the start and 0.075 at m = 300. So F′ increasing toward 0 means the truck uses less fuel per kilometer as the trip goes on. (The table is per kilometer; how fast fuel is used per hour also depends on the speed.) (B) reads 'F′ increases' as 'the amount used increases', ignoring the sign: F′ is getting closer to 0, so the loss per kilometer is shrinking. (C) confuses F decreasing (F′ < 0) with F′ decreasing (F″ < 0); a decreasing function can have an increasing derivative. (D) has concavity backward: a decreasing graph that is concave up levels off, falling less steeply.
parts.n: CHA-3.A.2, CHA-3.A.3 (topic 4.1); skill 3.F. Thinking: separate the sign of F′ (fuel is being used) from the change in F′ (how much is used per kilometer). Trap: (B), increasing derivative read as faster use.

parts.q:
The fuel left after 170 kilometers is estimated twice: once with the line tangent to the graph of F at m = 150, and once with the line tangent to the graph of F at m = 200. Which of the following is true?
(A) Both estimates are underestimates, so F(170) > 102.7.
(B) Both estimates are overestimates, so F(170) < 102.65.
(C) The estimate from m = 150 is too high and the one from m = 200 is too low, so 102.65 < F(170) < 102.7.
(D) The estimate from m = 150 is too low and the one from m = 200 is too high, so F(170) is between 102.65 and 102.7.
parts.a: (A). From m = 150: 104.5 + (−0.09)(20) = 102.7. From m = 200: 100.1 + (−0.085)(170 − 200) = 100.1 + 2.55 = 102.65. Because F″ > 0 on the whole interval, the graph of F is concave up and lies above each of its tangent lines, whichever side of the point of tangency you move to. So both values are underestimates, and F(170) is greater than the larger one, 102.7. (B) reverses the concavity rule. (C) assumes a tangent line used to the right of its point errs one way and one used to the left errs the other way; the direction of the error depends only on concavity. (D) makes the same assumption the other way round, and it cannot even be true: an underestimate of 102.7 and an overestimate of 102.65 would need F(170) > 102.7 and F(170) < 102.65 at once.
parts.n: CHA-3.F.1, CHA-3.F.2 (topic 4.6); skill 1.F. Thinking: compute both tangent-line values, then let the sign of F″ on the whole interval decide both errors. Trap: (C), which ties the direction of the error to the direction of the step.

mc.stem:
Questions 4-6 refer to the following.

A particle moves along the x-axis for 0 ≤ t ≤ 8. The graph of its position x(t) is smooth. The graph rises from (0, 2) to a peak at (1, 9), falls through (3, −7) to a low point at (5, −23), then rises to (8, 58). Its tangent line is horizontal at t = 1 and t = 5 and at no other time. The graph is concave down for 0 < t < 3 and concave up for 3 < t < 8.

parts.q:
On which of the following intervals is the particle moving to the left and slowing down?
(A) 0 < t < 1
(B) 1 < t < 3
(C) 3 < t < 5
(D) 5 < t < 8
parts.a: (C). Moving left means x is decreasing, so v(t) < 0: that is 1 < t < 5. Slowing down means v and a have opposite signs; with v < 0 that needs a > 0, which is where the graph is concave up: 3 < t < 8. Both hold on 3 < t < 5. (A) is an interval where the particle is slowing down (v > 0, a < 0), but it is moving to the right there. (B) is moving left, but a < 0 there (concave down), so v and a are both negative and the particle is speeding up; a negative acceleration does not by itself mean slowing down. (D) has a > 0, but v > 0 as well, so the particle is moving right and speeding up.
parts.n: CHA-3.B.1 (topic 4.2); skill 2.B. Thinking: read the sign of v from where the graph rises or falls and the sign of a from its concavity, then compare the two signs. Trap: (B), negative acceleration read as slowing down.

parts.q:
A student says, "At t = 4 the velocity is negative and the acceleration is positive, so the particle is slowing down and heading back toward the origin." Which of the following best evaluates the student's statement?
(A) It is correct: a particle that is slowing down is turning around, so it is returning toward the origin.
(B) It is partly wrong: the particle is slowing down, but x(4) < 0 and v(4) < 0, so it is moving away from the origin.
(C) It is partly wrong: the particle is moving toward the origin, but a positive acceleration means it is speeding up.
(D) It is correct: the velocity is negative at t = 4, and a negative velocity means the particle moves toward the origin.
parts.a: (B). At t = 4 the graph is falling (v < 0) and concave up (a > 0), so the speed is decreasing: that half is right. But between t = 3 and t = 5 the position is between −7 and −23, so x(4) < 0, and the particle is moving in the negative direction, farther from 0. The distance from the origin increases when x and v have the same sign. (A) treats slowing down as turning around; the particle does not turn until t = 5, and it moves away from the origin until then. (C) reverses the speed rule: with v < 0 and a > 0 the signs differ, so the particle is slowing down. (D) equates negative velocity with moving toward the origin; that is true only for a particle to the right of the origin.
parts.n: CHA-3.B.1 (topic 4.2); skill 3.E. Thinking: toward or away from the origin depends on the signs of x and v, while speeding up or slowing down depends on the signs of v and a. Trap: (D), negative velocity read as 'toward the origin'.

parts.q:
What is the total distance the particle travels from t = 0 to t = 8?
(A) 56
(B) 97
(C) 106
(D) 120
parts.a: (D). The particle changes direction only where v changes sign, at t = 1 (the peak) and t = 5 (the low point), so split the trip there: from 2 to 9 is 7 units, from 9 to −23 is 32 units, and from −23 to 58 is 81 units, for 7 + 32 + 81 = 120. (A) is the displacement, x(8) − x(0) = 58 − 2 = 56, which lets the leftward trip cancel part of the rightward ones. (B) takes the last leg as 58, the final position, instead of the change 58 − (−23) = 81. (C) misses the turn at t = 1, measuring |−23 − 2| = 25 for the first part (the same total comes from splitting at the inflection point t = 3 instead of at t = 1); the particle goes out to 9 and back, which adds 14.
parts.n: CHA-3.B.1 (topic 4.2); skill 2.B. Thinking: find the turning points from the graph and add the distance of each leg. Trap: (A), displacement for distance.

mc.stem:
Questions 7-9 refer to the following.

A water trough is 6 meters long. Its ends are triangles with a horizontal top edge 2 meters wide and a vertex 1 meter directly below the middle of the top edge, so the trough is 1 meter deep. Water flows in at a constant 0.3 cubic meter per minute. A student finds how fast the water level is rising when the water is 0.5 meter deep. The student's work is shown.
Line 1: With depth h and water-surface width w, the volume is V = (1/2)(w)(h)(6) = 3wh.
Line 2: When h = 0.5, the width of the water surface is w = 1, so V = 3h.
Line 3: dV/dt = 3(dh/dt).
Line 4: 0.3 = 3(dh/dt), so the level rises at 0.1 meter per minute.

parts.q:
Which of the following identifies the first error in the student's work and gives the correct rate?
(A) Line 2: w changes as h changes (w = 2h), so V = 6h²; the correct rate is 0.05 meter per minute.
(B) Line 1: the volume of the trough is (w)(h)(6) = 6wh with no factor 1/2; the correct rate is 0.025 meter per minute.
(C) Line 3: V = 3h is a product, so dV/dt = 3h(dh/dt); the correct rate is 0.2 meter per minute.
(D) There is no error: at the instant h = 0.5 the surface is 1 meter wide, so the rate is 0.1 meter per minute.
parts.a: (A). By similar triangles the water surface is 2 meters wide when the depth is 1 meter, so w = 2h at every depth. Line 2 fixes w at its value for one instant before differentiating, which throws away the way w grows as the water rises. Correctly, V = (1/2)(2h)(h)(6) = 6h², dV/dt = 12h(dh/dt), and at h = 0.5: 0.3 = 6(dh/dt), so dh/dt = 0.05 meter per minute. (B) drops the 1/2 from the triangle's area; Line 1 is right, since the cross-section is a triangle. (C) finds a false error in Line 3: 3 is a constant, so the derivative of 3h with respect to t is 3(dh/dt), and 3h(dh/dt) with h = 0.5 gives 0.2. The real problem is earlier: Line 2 should never have made V linear in h. (D) defends substituting a value before differentiating; a quantity that is changing must stay a variable until after the derivative is taken.
parts.n: CHA-3.D.1, CHA-3.E.1 (topic 4.5); skill 3.G. Thinking: check each line for a quantity frozen at its instantaneous value before differentiating. Trap: (D), 'w really is 1 at that instant'.

parts.q:
Water keeps flowing in at 0.3 cubic meter per minute. As the depth increases from 0.5 meter to 1 meter, what happens to the rate at which the water level rises, and why?
(A) It decreases, because the water surface widens as h grows, so each cubic meter raises the level less.
(B) It stays 0.05 meter per minute, because water flows into the trough at a constant rate.
(C) It increases, because dV/dt = 12h(dh/dt), so dh/dt grows in proportion to the depth h.
(D) It decreases, because the volume 6h² keeps growing, so the inflow rate dV/dt must drop as well.
parts.a: (A). From dV/dt = 12h(dh/dt), dh/dt = 0.3/(12h) = 0.025/h, which falls from 0.05 at h = 0.5 to 0.025 at h = 1. The reason is geometric: the surface is 2h meters wide and 6 meters long, 12h square meters in all, and a fixed inflow spread over a larger surface raises the level more slowly. (B) assumes a constant inflow gives a constant rise; that is true only for a container with vertical sides. (C) solves 0.3 = 12h(dh/dt) the wrong way round; h multiplies dh/dt, so dh/dt is proportional to 1/h. (D) has the right prediction for a false reason: dV/dt is the inflow, which stays 0.3 cubic meter per minute.
parts.n: CHA-3.E.1 (topic 4.5); skill 3.F. Thinking: solve the related-rates equation for dh/dt as a function of h and explain the trend by the widening surface. Trap: (B), constant inflow read as constant rise.

parts.q:
Suppose the trough's triangular ends were 3 meters wide across the top instead of 2 meters, still 1 meter deep, with the same length and the same inflow. How fast would the water level rise when the water is 0.5 meter deep?
(A) 1/20 meter per minute
(B) 1/15 meter per minute
(C) 1/30 meter per minute
(D) 3/40 meter per minute
parts.a: (C). Now the surface width is w = 3h, the cross-section has area (1/2)(3h)(h) = 1.5h², and V = 9h². Then dV/dt = 18h(dh/dt); at h = 0.5, 0.3 = 9(dh/dt), so dh/dt = 1/30 meter per minute. A wider trough spreads the inflow over more surface, so the level rises more slowly than 1/20. (A) is the answer for the original trough; the rate depends on the width of the water surface, not only on the depth. (B) repeats the student's error from Line 2, freezing the width at 1.5 meters: V = 4.5h gives 0.3/4.5 = 1/15. (D) scales the original rate up by 3/2, but a wider surface makes the level rise more slowly, so the rate is scaled by 2/3.
parts.n: CHA-3.D.1 (topic 4.4); skill 1.E. Thinking: rebuild the volume relation for the new shape, differentiate with respect to t, then substitute. Trap: (D), scaling the rate the wrong way.

parts.q:
A student evaluates $\lim_{x \to 0} \frac{1 - \cos 2x}{x^{2} + 3x}$. The student's work is shown.
Line 1: As x → 0, 1 − cos 2x → 0 and x² + 3x → 0, so the limit has the form 0/0.
Line 2: By L'Hospital's Rule, the limit equals $\lim_{x \to 0} \frac{2\sin 2x}{2x + 3}$.
Line 3: By L'Hospital's Rule again, this equals $\lim_{x \to 0} \frac{4\cos 2x}{2}$.
Line 4: So the limit is 4/2 = 2.
Which of the following best evaluates the student's work?
(A) Line 2 is wrong: the derivative of 1 − cos 2x is −2 sin 2x, so the limit is −2.
(B) Line 3 is wrong: the limit in Line 2 has the form 0/3, not 0/0, so the limit is 0.
(C) Line 2 is wrong: the rule calls for the quotient rule, applied to the whole fraction.
(D) There is no error: each use of L'Hospital's Rule was justified, so the limit is 2.
parts.a: (B). Lines 1 and 2 are correct: the form is 0/0, and the derivative of 1 − cos 2x is 2 sin 2x. But in Line 2, as x → 0 the numerator 2 sin 2x → 0 and the denominator 2x + 3 → 3, so the limit is 0/3 = 0. That is not an indeterminate form, so L'Hospital's Rule does not apply a second time; using it anyway gives the wrong value 2. (A) makes a sign error: the derivative of −cos 2x is +2 sin 2x (and even with the sign error, the limit would still be 0). (C) confuses L'Hospital's Rule with the derivative of a quotient; the rule differentiates the numerator and the denominator separately. (D) accepts the second use of the rule without checking its form; the check in Line 1 has to be repeated before each use.
parts.n: LIM-4.A.1, LIM-4.A.2 (topic 4.7); skill 3.D. Thinking: re-check the form before each use of L'Hospital's Rule. Trap: (D), applying the rule twice because it worked once.

parts.q:
A limit of the form 0/0 can hide conditions on its constants. For which constants a and b is $\lim_{x \to 0} \frac{e^{2x} - a - bx}{x^{2}}$ a finite number, and what is that number?
(A) a = 1 and b = 2; the limit is 4
(B) a = 1 and b = 1; the limit is 1/2
(C) a = 1 and b = 2; the limit is 2
(D) a = 1 and b is any number; the limit is 2
parts.a: (C). The denominator → 0, so a finite limit needs the numerator → 0 as well: 1 − a = 0, a = 1. Then the form is 0/0, and L'Hospital's Rule gives $\lim_{x \to 0} \frac{2e^{2x} - b}{2x}$. The denominator → 0 again, so again the numerator must → 0: 2 − b = 0, b = 2. The form is 0/0 once more, and a second use gives $\lim_{x \to 0} \frac{4e^{2x}}{2}$ = 2. (A) forgets to divide by the 2 from differentiating 2x in the last step. (B) drops the chain rule, treating the derivative of $e^{2x}$ as $e^{2x}$: that gives b = 1 and 1/2. (D) differentiates twice without checking the middle form; if b ≠ 2, then $(2e^{2x} - b)/(2x)$ has the form (2 − b)/0 and the limit is not finite.
parts.n: LIM-4.A.1, LIM-4.A.2 (topic 4.7), with the limit reasoning of unit 1; skill 3.D. Thinking: a finite limit with a denominator → 0 forces the numerator → 0, at each stage. Trap: (D), skipping the check at the middle stage.

parts.q:
A camera on level ground is 400 meters from a rocket's launch pad and turns to keep the rocket in view. The rocket rises straight up at a constant 50 meters per second. Let θ be the camera's angle of elevation, in radians. A student says, "The rocket rises at a constant rate, so θ increases at a constant rate." Which of the following best evaluates the student's statement?
(A) It is correct: θ depends only on the height h, and h changes at a constant rate, so θ changes at a constant rate.
(B) It is wrong: dθ/dt = 0.125 sec²θ, which grows as the rocket rises, so the camera turns faster and faster.
(C) It is correct: differentiating tan θ = h/400 gives dθ/dt = (dh/dt)/400 = 0.125 radian per second at every height.
(D) It is wrong: dθ/dt = 0.125 cos²θ, which shrinks as the rocket rises; it is 0.0625 radian per second when h = 400.
parts.a: (D). tan θ = h/400. Differentiating with respect to t: sec²θ(dθ/dt) = (1/400)(dh/dt) = 50/400, so dθ/dt = 0.125cos²θ. As the rocket rises, θ grows toward π/2 and cos²θ shrinks: dθ/dt is 0.125 radian per second at liftoff and 0.125(1/2) = 0.0625 when h = 400 (θ = π/4). Equal climbs of the rocket turn the camera through smaller and smaller angles. (A) assumes that a function of a steadily changing quantity changes steadily; that holds only when the function is linear, and θ = arctan(h/400) is not. (B) solves for dθ/dt incorrectly, multiplying by sec²θ instead of dividing by it. (C) differentiates tan θ as if it were θ, leaving out the factor sec²θ from the chain rule.
parts.n: CHA-3.E.1 (topic 4.5); skill 3.F. Thinking: find dθ/dt as a function of θ and see how it changes as the rocket rises. Trap: (C), dropping sec²θ.

parts.q:
A farm's corn harvest is H = YA bushels, where Y is the yield in bushels per acre and A is the number of acres planted, both differentiable functions of time t in years. Right now Y = 180 and is increasing at 3 bushels per acre per year, and A = 400 and is decreasing at 10 acres per year. At this moment, how is the harvest changing?
(A) Decreasing at 30 bushels per year, the product of the two rates of change
(B) Decreasing at 600 bushels per year: the loss from acres outweighs the gain from yield
(C) Increasing at 1,200 bushels per year, because the yield per acre is going up
(D) Increasing at 3,000 bushels per year, because both changes add to the harvest
parts.a: (B). By the product rule, dH/dt = (dY/dt)A + Y(dA/dt) = (3)(400) + (180)(−10) = 1200 − 1800 = −600 bushels per year. The higher yield on the current acres adds 1,200 bushels a year, but the lost acres, each yielding 180 bushels, take away 1,800. (A) multiplies the two rates, as if the derivative of a product were the product of the derivatives. (C) keeps only the yield term and ignores that fewer acres are planted. (D) adds the sizes of the two terms, dropping the negative sign of dA/dt.
parts.n: CHA-3.C.1, CHA-3.D.2 (topic 4.3); skill 1.E. Thinking: use the product rule on a total that is the product of two changing quantities, and weigh the two terms. Trap: (A), the product of the rates.

parts.q:
A metal part is taken out of an oven. Its temperature T(t), in degrees Celsius, t minutes later satisfies T(10) = 82 and T′(10) = −1.6, and T″(t) > 0 for all t > 0. A technician uses the line tangent to the graph of T at t = 10 to predict when the part will cool to 75°C. Which of the following gives the prediction and compares it with the actual time?
(A) t ≈ 14.4 minutes; the part actually reaches 75°C later than that
(B) t ≈ 14.4 minutes; the part actually reaches 75°C earlier than that
(C) t ≈ 21.2 minutes; the part actually reaches 75°C later than that
(D) t ≈ 21.2 minutes; the part actually reaches 75°C earlier than that
parts.a: (A). The tangent line is y = 82 − 1.6(t − 10). Setting y = 75 gives t − 10 = 7/1.6 = 4.375, so t ≈ 14.4 minutes. Because T″ > 0, the graph of T is concave up and lies above its tangent line, so at t = 14.375 the actual temperature is still above 75°C: the cooling slows down, and the part reaches 75°C later than predicted. (B) knows the tangent line lies below the graph but turns that into the wrong conclusion about time: a temperature that is higher than predicted takes longer, not less time, to fall to 75. (C) and (D) multiply 7 by 1.6 instead of dividing, getting 10 + 11.2 = 21.2; a drop of 7 degrees at 1.6 degrees per minute takes 7/1.6 minutes.
parts.n: CHA-3.F.1, CHA-3.F.2 (topic 4.6); skill 1.F. Thinking: use the tangent line backward to predict a time, then turn 'the graph is above the tangent line' into 'later'. Trap: (B), which turns 'underestimate' into 'earlier'.

parts.q:
Let C(d) be the concentration of a medicine in a patient's blood, in milligrams per liter, 2 hours after a dose of d milligrams. For this patient C(200) = 1.8 and C′(200) = 0.015. The doctor wants the concentration 2 hours after the dose to be about 2.1 milligrams per liter. Using local linearity at d = 200, which dose should the doctor choose?
(A) 200.0045 milligrams
(B) 140 milligrams
(C) 220 milligrams
(D) 20 milligrams
parts.a: (C). C′(200) = 0.015 means that, near a 200-milligram dose, each extra milligram of dose raises the 2-hour concentration by about 0.015 milligram per liter (the units of C′ are milligrams per liter per milligram of dose). Raising the concentration by 2.1 − 1.8 = 0.3 takes about 0.3/0.015 = 20 more milligrams: the tangent line 1.8 + 0.015(d − 200) = 2.1 gives d = 220 milligrams. (A) multiplies the needed change by C′ instead of dividing, 200 + (0.3)(0.015). (B) treats the concentration as proportional to the dose, 2.1/0.015; the tangent line passes through (200, 1.8), not through the origin. (D) finds the extra dose, 20 milligrams, and gives it as the whole dose.
parts.n: CHA-3.A.2, CHA-3.A.3 (topic 4.1), with local linearity (topic 4.6); skill 1.D. Thinking: read C′ as 'change in output per unit of input' when the input is a dose, not a time, and solve the tangent line for the input. Trap: (B), proportional reasoning through the origin.

parts.q:
The pressure P, in atmospheres, and the volume V, in liters, of a gas in a cylinder with a moving piston satisfy PV = 24. At one instant V = 4 and V is increasing at 0.5 liter per minute. A student says, "PV stays constant, so P must be decreasing at 0.5 atmosphere per minute at that instant." Which of the following best evaluates the student's statement?
(A) It is correct: when a product stays constant, a gain in one factor is matched by an equal loss in the other.
(B) It is wrong: by the product rule, P′V + PV′ = 0, so P′ = −0.75 atmosphere per minute at that instant.
(C) It is wrong: differentiating PV = 24 gives P′V′ = 0, so P is not changing at all at that instant.
(D) It is wrong: since P = 24/V, P′ = −24/V² = −1.5 atmospheres per minute at that instant.
parts.a: (B). Differentiate PV = 24 with respect to t, using the product rule: (dP/dt)V + P(dV/dt) = 0. At the instant, V = 4 and P = 24/4 = 6, so 4(dP/dt) + 6(0.5) = 0 and dP/dt = −0.75 atmosphere per minute. The rates are not equal and opposite; each is weighted by the other quantity's size. (A) treats a constant product like a constant sum; only for P + V = constant would the rates be equal and opposite. (C) differentiates a product as the product of the derivatives. (D) differentiates 24/V with respect to V but forgets the chain-rule factor dV/dt = 0.5; the correct value is (−24/16)(0.5) = −0.75.
parts.n: CHA-3.D.1, CHA-3.D.2 (topic 4.4); skill 3.G. Thinking: differentiate the relation with respect to time, product rule and all, before substituting. Trap: (A), a constant product treated like a constant sum.

mc.stem:
Questions 17-19 refer to the following.

Particles P and Q move along the x-axis. For 0 ≤ t ≤ 5 seconds, their positions, in meters, are $x_{P}(t) = 5te^{-0.4t}$ and $x_{Q}(t) = 3 + 2\cos(1.3t)$.

parts.q:
At time t = 4, which of the following describes the motion of each particle?
(A) P is moving left and slowing down; Q is moving right and slowing down.
(B) P is moving left and speeding up; Q is moving left and speeding up.
(C) P is moving left and slowing down; Q is moving right and speeding up.
(D) P is moving left and speeding up; Q is moving right and slowing down.
parts.a: (D). With a calculator, $v_{P}(4) = x_{P}'(4) \approx -0.606$ and $a_{P}(4) \approx -0.162$: P moves left, and because its velocity and acceleration have the same sign, it is speeding up. $v_{Q}(4) \approx 2.297$ and $a_{Q}(4) \approx -1.584$: Q moves right, and because the signs differ, it is slowing down. (A) reads a negative acceleration as slowing down for both particles; P's velocity is negative too, so P is speeding up. (B) comes from a calculator in degree mode, which makes both $v_{Q}(4)$ and $a_{Q}(4)$ negative; the model's angles are in radians. (C) reverses the rule: matching signs of velocity and acceleration mean speeding up, and opposite signs mean slowing down.
parts.n: CHA-3.B.1 (topic 4.2); skill 1.E. Thinking: compute v and a for each particle at the same instant and compare their signs particle by particle. Trap: (A), negative acceleration read as slowing down.

parts.q:
At what time t, for 0 < t < 5, are the two particles moving in the same direction with the same speed?
(A) t ≈ 1.041
(B) t ≈ 2.392
(C) t ≈ 2.432
(D) t ≈ 3.680
parts.a: (C). Same direction and same speed means the same velocity: $v_{P}(t) = v_{Q}(t)$, that is, $(5 - 2t)e^{-0.4t} = -2.6\sin(1.3t)$. Graphing the difference of the two velocities on 0 < t < 5 shows one zero, at t ≈ 2.432, where both velocities are about 0.051 meter per second. (A) solves $x_{P}(t) = x_{Q}(t)$: at t ≈ 1.041 the particles are at the same place, passing each other, which says nothing about their velocities. (B) solves $v_{P}(t) = -v_{Q}(t)$: the speeds are equal there, but the particles move in opposite directions. (D) solves $a_{P}(t) = a_{Q}(t)$, matching the accelerations instead of the velocities.
parts.n: CHA-3.B.1 (topic 4.2); skill 1.E. Thinking: turn 'same direction, same speed' into equal velocities and solve with the calculator. Trap: (A), same position read as same motion.

parts.q:
A student says, "At t = 3, particle Q is moving faster than particle P, so the distance between them is increasing at the difference of their speeds, about 1.487 meters per second." Which of the following best evaluates the student's statement?
(A) It is correct: the distance between two particles changes at the difference of their speeds, 1.788 − 0.301 ≈ 1.487.
(B) It is wrong: Q is to the left of P and moving right while P moves left, so the distance is decreasing at about 2.089.
(C) It is wrong: the distance is decreasing, not increasing, but its rate is the difference of the speeds, about 1.487.
(D) It is wrong: the particles move in opposite directions, so they separate, and the distance is increasing at about 2.089.
parts.a: (B). At t = 3, $x_{P}(3) \approx 4.518$ and $x_{Q}(3) \approx 1.548$, so P is to the right of Q and the distance is $d(t) = x_{P}(t) - x_{Q}(t)$ near t = 3. Then $d'(3) = v_{P}(3) - v_{Q}(3) \approx -0.301 - 1.788 = -2.089$: Q moves right toward P and P moves left toward Q, so the gap closes at about 2.089 meters per second. (A) subtracts the speeds, which is right only when the particles move in the same direction. (C) gets the direction right but keeps the student's difference of speeds; with the particles approaching each other the speeds add. (D) assumes that opposite directions mean moving apart; whether the gap opens or closes depends on which particle is on which side.
parts.n: CHA-3.B.1 (topic 4.2); skill 3.E. Thinking: write the distance as $x_{P} - x_{Q}$ from the positions, then differentiate, rather than combining speeds by instinct. Trap: (D), opposite directions read as separating.

mc.stem:
Questions 20-21 refer to the following.

Sand is poured onto a pile shaped like a cone. The radius of the pile's base is always 1.5 times the pile's height. Sand is added at the rate R(t) = 12 + 4sin(0.3t) cubic feet per minute, where t is measured in minutes, and no sand is lost. At time t = 5, the pile is 4 feet high. The volume of a cone with base radius r and height h is $V = \frac{1}{3}\pi r^{2}h$.

parts.q:
At time t = 5, at what rate, in feet per minute, is the height of the pile increasing?
(A) 0.047
(B) 0.107
(C) 0.141
(D) 0.716
parts.a: (C). With r = 1.5h, $V = \frac{1}{3}\pi (1.5h)^{2}h = 0.75\pi h^{3}$, so dV/dt = 2.25πh²(dh/dt). The volume grows at the rate sand is added: dV/dt = R(5) = 12 + 4sin(1.5) ≈ 15.990. At h = 4, 36π(dh/dt) = 15.990, so dh/dt ≈ 0.141 foot per minute. (A) uses the volume of a cylinder, πr²h, which is three times too large, so the height seems to rise a third as fast. (B) evaluates sin(1.5) with the calculator in degree mode, which gives R(5) ≈ 12.105. (D) flips the ratio, writing r = h/1.5; that is a pile whose base is narrower than it is tall, so the same sand raises it much faster.
parts.n: CHA-3.E.1 (topic 4.5); skill 1.E. Thinking: use the fixed shape to write V in terms of h alone, differentiate with respect to t, and let the rate function supply dV/dt. Trap: (B), degree mode.

parts.q:
A student notices that R′(t) > 0 for 0 ≤ t ≤ 5 and says, "Sand is being added faster and faster, so at t = 5 the height of the pile is rising faster and faster." Which of the following best evaluates the student's statement?
(A) It is correct: R′(5) ≈ 0.085 > 0, and a larger inflow of sand always makes the height of the pile rise at a larger rate.
(B) It is wrong: differentiating R = 2.25πh²(dh/dt) with respect to t gives d²h/dt² ≈ −0.009 at t = 5.
(C) It is wrong: differentiating R = 2.25πh²(dh/dt) with respect to t gives d²h/dt² ≈ −0.070 at t = 5.
(D) It is correct: differentiating R = 2.25πh²(dh/dt) with respect to t gives d²h/dt² ≈ 0.001 at t = 5.
parts.a: (B). Differentiate R(t) = 2.25πh²(dh/dt) with the product and chain rules: R′(t) = 4.5πh(dh/dt)² + 2.25πh²(d²h/dt²). At t = 5, R′(5) = 1.2cos(1.5) ≈ 0.0849, h = 4 and dh/dt ≈ 0.14138, so 0.0849 ≈ 1.1303 + 36π(d²h/dt²), and d²h/dt² ≈ −0.009. The rise is slowing down: the extra sand each minute is small next to the growth of the pile it has to cover. (A) assumes that more sand per minute means a faster rise, ignoring that the pile widens as it grows. (C) reaches the right verdict with a slip: it writes the derivative of h² as 2h instead of 2h(dh/dt), which gives (0.0849 − 4.5π(4)(0.14138))/(36π) ≈ −0.070. (D) treats h² as a constant, so d²h/dt² = R′(5)/(36π) ≈ 0.00075; but h is changing, and its change is what slows the rise.
parts.n: CHA-3.D.1, CHA-3.D.2 (topic 4.4), with CHA-3.E.1 (topic 4.5); skill 3.G. Thinking: differentiate the related-rates equation a second time, product rule included, to decide whether the rate itself is growing. Trap: (A), a growing inflow read as a growing rate of rise.

parts.q:
The concentration of a drug in a patient's blood is $C(t) = 20te^{-t/2}$ milligrams per liter, t hours after an injection. A student estimates C(5) with the line tangent to the graph of C at t = 3.8. The student's work is shown.
Line 1: C(3.8) ≈ 11.367 and C′(3.8) ≈ −2.692.
Line 2: The tangent line is y = 11.367 − 2.692(t − 3.8), so C(5) ≈ 8.137.
Line 3: C″(3.8) ≈ −0.150, so the graph of C is concave down at t = 3.8.
Line 4: So 8.137 is an overestimate of C(5).
Which of the following best evaluates the student's work?
(A) There is no error: C″(3.8) < 0, so the graph lies below its tangent line and 8.137 is an overestimate.
(B) Line 3 is the first error: C″(3.8) ≈ 0.150 > 0, so the graph is concave up and 8.137 is an underestimate.
(C) Line 4 is the first error: C″(5) ≈ 0.410 > 0, and the concavity at t = 5 decides, so 8.137 is an underestimate.
(D) Line 4 is the first error: C″ changes sign at t = 4, and C(5) ≈ 8.208, so 8.137 is an underestimate.
parts.a: (D). Lines 1 to 3 are correct. But $C''(t) = 5e^{-t/2}(t - 4)$ is negative for t < 4 and positive for t > 4, so the graph changes concavity at t = 4, between 3.8 and 5. The concavity at the point of tangency decides the error only when it holds on the whole interval. Here the calculator gives C(5) = $100e^{-2.5}$ ≈ 8.208 > 8.137, so the tangent line gives an underestimate: the concave-up stretch after t = 4 bends the graph back above the line. (A) accepts Line 4, reasoning from the concavity at one point. (B) makes a sign slip in C″(3.8); Line 3 is right, C″(3.8) ≈ −0.150.
