(C) reaches the right verdict by the same faulty rule the student used, only at the other end: the concavity at t = 5 alone does not decide either, since the graph is concave down on part of the interval.
parts.n: CHA-3.F.2 (topic 4.6), with FUN-4.A.6 (topic 5.6); skill 1.F. Thinking: check the sign of C″ on the whole interval between the point of tangency and the estimate, and settle the case with the calculator. Trap: (A), concavity at the point of tangency taken as enough.

parts.q:
On a day when the air temperature stays at 10°F, a weather service models the wind chill, in degrees Fahrenheit, as $W(v) = 41.955 - 31.475v^{0.16}$, where v is the wind speed in miles per hour. At a moment when the wind speed is 20 miles per hour and is increasing at 3 miles per hour per hour, at what rate is the wind chill changing, in degrees Fahrenheit per hour?
(A) −1.220
(B) −1.149
(C) −0.407
(D) −0.136
parts.a: (A). The wind chill depends on time through the wind speed, so by the chain rule dW/dt = W′(v)·(dv/dt). With the calculator, W′(20) ≈ −0.4066 degree per mile per hour of wind speed, so dW/dt ≈ (−0.4066)(3) ≈ −1.220 degrees Fahrenheit per hour. The units check: (degrees per mph)(mph per hour) = degrees per hour. (B) computes W(23) − W(20), the change over the next hour if the wind kept speeding up at 3 miles per hour per hour; that is an average rate over an hour, not the rate at this moment. (C) is W′(20), the rate per mile per hour of wind speed; it never uses how fast the wind is changing. (D) divides W′(20) by 3 instead of multiplying, which leaves the wrong units.
parts.n: CHA-3.C.1 (topic 4.3), with CHA-3.A.3 (topic 4.1); skill 1.E. Thinking: turn a rate with respect to wind speed into a rate with respect to time, letting the units choose the operation. Trap: (C), stopping at dW/dv.

parts.q:
An oil slick spreads on calm water as a circle. Its radius, in meters, t hours after a leak begins is r(t) = 50arctan(0.4t). Which of the following correctly compares how the slick is growing at t = 2 hours with how it was growing at t = 1 hour?
(A) The radius and the area are both growing faster at t = 2 than at t = 1.
(B) The radius and the area are both growing more slowly at t = 2 than at t = 1.
(C) The radius is growing faster at t = 2, but the area is growing more slowly.
(D) The radius is growing more slowly at t = 2, but the area is growing faster.
parts.a: (D). r′(t) = 20/(1 + 0.16t²), so r′(1) ≈ 17.241 and r′(2) ≈ 12.195 meters per hour: the radius grows more slowly. For the area A = πr², dA/dt = 2πr(dr/dt). With the calculator, r(1) ≈ 19.025 and r(2) ≈ 33.737, so dA/dt ≈ 2061.0 square meters per hour at t = 1 and ≈ 2585.1 at t = 2: the area grows faster. The edge of the slick is longer at t = 2, so a slower outward spread still adds more area each hour. (A) compares the radii themselves: r(2) > r(1) says the slick is bigger, not that the radius is growing faster. (B) assumes the area's rate follows the radius's rate; that drops the factor r from dA/dt = 2πr(dr/dt), and r grew from about 19.0 to 33.7. (C) has both comparisons backward: it reads the bigger radius as faster growth and then drops the factor r for the area.
parts.n: CHA-3.D.1 (topic 4.4); skill 2.B. Thinking: compute each rate separately and see that dA/dt depends on the size of r as well as on dr/dt. Trap: (B), area and radius assumed to speed up or slow down together.

fr.title: A diver's descent: depth, temperature and a dive computer's forecast
fr.stem:
A diver descends from the surface of a lake. Her depth, in meters, t minutes after she starts is $D(t) = \frac{30t^{3}}{t^{3} + 64}$ for 0 ≤ t ≤ 10. The water temperature at a depth of d meters is $W(d) = 4 + 18e^{-0.05d}$ degrees Celsius.
A graphing calculator is allowed.

parts.q: Find W′(10). Using correct units, interpret the meaning of W′(10) in the context of the problem.
parts.a: $W'(10) = -0.9e^{-0.5}$ ≈ −0.546 degree Celsius per meter (1 point). At a depth of 10 meters, the water temperature is decreasing at a rate of about 0.546 degree Celsius per meter of additional depth (1 point).
parts.n: 'The temperature drops 0.546 degree per minute' uses the wrong units: W is a function of depth, not time, so this loses the interpretation point. So does 'at 10 meters the water is 0.546 degree colder', which reads a rate as an amount.

parts.q: Let T(t) = W(D(t)) be the water temperature at the diver's location at time t. Find T′(2.5). Using correct units, explain what your answer says about the water around the diver at t = 2.5.
parts.a: By the chain rule, T′(2.5) = W′(D(2.5))·D′(2.5) (1 point). With D(2.5) ≈ 5.887 and D′(2.5) ≈ 5.678, T′(2.5) ≈ (−0.6705)(5.678) ≈ −3.807 degrees Celsius per minute: at t = 2.5 minutes the water around the diver is getting colder at about 3.807 degrees Celsius per minute (1 point).
parts.n: W′(2.5)·D′(2.5) ≈ −4.510, which uses the time 2.5 as a depth, earns only the chain-rule point if the form W′(D(t))D′(t) is written. W′(D(2.5)) alone, in degrees per meter, earns nothing.

parts.q: At t = 4, the diver's dive computer predicts her depth half a minute later using the line tangent to the graph of D at t = 4. Find the computer's prediction. Is the prediction too deep or too shallow? Give a reason for your answer.
parts.a: D(4) = 15 and D′(4) = 5.625, so the prediction is 15 + 5.625(0.5) = 17.8125 ≈ 17.813 meters (1 point). It is too deep, an overestimate: D″(t) < 0 for 4 ≤ t ≤ 4.5 (the calculator gives D″(4) ≈ −1.406 and shows D″ negative on the whole interval; D″ < 0 for all t > ∛32), so the graph of D is concave down there and lies below its tangent line (1 point). (Check: D(4.5) ≈ 17.623.)
parts.n: 'Too deep, because she is slowing down' earns the point only if it is tied to D′ decreasing on [4, 4.5]; 'too deep because D″(4) < 0' with no mention of the interval earns nothing for the reason. Computing D(4.5) and comparing is a check, not the reason the question asks for, unless the concavity is also given.

parts.q: The diver descends fastest at t = ∛32 ≈ 3.175 minutes, when she is 10 meters deep. A student says, "The water around her gets colder fastest when she descends fastest, so T′(t) is most negative at t = 3.175." Do you agree? Justify your answer.
parts.a: No, I disagree (1 point for the conclusion with a supporting computation). T′(3.175) = W′(10)·D′(3.175) ≈ (−0.5459)(6.300) ≈ −3.439 degrees Celsius per minute (1 point), but T′(2.5) ≈ −3.807 from part (b) is more negative, so the temperature around her is falling faster at t = 2.5 than at t = 3.175. The reason is that T′(t) = W′(D(t))·D′(t) is a product: the water cools less per meter the deeper she goes (|W′(d)| = $0.9e^{-0.05d}$ decreases as d increases), so the product is largest before her descent is fastest (1 point for the explanation). (The calculator places the most negative T′ near t ≈ 2.568.)
parts.n: Agreeing because 'T′ is a multiple of D′' earns nothing: the multiplier W′(D(t)) changes with time. A bare 'No' earns nothing; a comparison of T′ at two times, or an explanation of the changing factor W′(D(t)), is needed.

fr.title: A shadow on a wall: a related rate, a student's sign and a faster walk
fr.stem:
A spotlight sits on level ground 20 meters from a vertical wall and shines toward the wall. A person 2 meters tall walks in a straight line from the spotlight toward the wall at a constant 1.5 meters per second, casting a shadow on the wall. Let x be the person's distance from the spotlight and S the height of the shadow on the wall, both in meters, at time t seconds.
A calculator is not allowed.

parts.q: Find the rate at which the height of the shadow is changing when the person is 8 meters from the spotlight. Indicate units of measure.
parts.a: By similar triangles (the light ray from the spotlight passes over the person's head to the top of the shadow), S/20 = 2/x, so S = 40/x (1 point). Differentiating with respect to t: dS/dt = −(40/x²)(dx/dt) (1 point). At x = 8 with dx/dt = 1.5: dS/dt = −(40/64)(1.5) = −0.9375 meter per second; the shadow is getting shorter at 0.9375 meter per second (1 point).
parts.n: S/x = 2/20 (the triangles matched the wrong way) gives S = x/10 and a growing shadow, and earns nothing after the first step. Substituting x = 8 before differentiating gives dS/dt = 0 and earns only the relation point.

parts.q:
A student measures from the wall instead. The student's work is shown.
Line 1: Let y = 20 − x be the person's distance from the wall. Then S = 40/(20 − y).
Line 2: dS/dt = [40/(20 − y)²](dy/dt).
Line 3: When the person is 8 meters from the spotlight, y = 12 and dy/dt = 1.5, so dS/dt = (40/64)(1.5) = 0.9375.
Line 4: The shadow is growing at 0.9375 meter per second.
Is the student's reasoning correct? If not, identify the error and explain how the answer shows it.
parts.a: No (1 point for identifying the error). Lines 1 and 2 are correct, but in Line 3 dy/dt = −1.5, because the person's distance from the wall is decreasing. With dy/dt = −1.5, dS/dt = −0.9375, which agrees with part (a). The answer itself signals the error (1 point for the explanation): as the person approaches the wall, x increases, so S = 40/x must decrease; a growing shadow contradicts the geometry.
parts.n: 'The student should have used x instead of y' earns nothing: y works as well as x. Calling Line 2 wrong earns nothing; the chain rule there is correct, and the only error is the sign of dy/dt.

parts.q: As the person keeps walking toward the wall, does the shadow shrink faster or more slowly? Justify your answer.
parts.a: More slowly (1 point). With dx/dt = 1.5, dS/dt = −60/x², so the shadow shrinks at 60/x² meters per second, which decreases as x increases toward 20 (1 point for the justification). Equivalently, d²S/dt² = (120/x³)(dx/dt) = 180/x³ > 0: dS/dt is negative and increasing toward 0. At x = 8 the rate is 0.9375; at x = 15 it is 60/225 ≈ 0.267.
parts.n: 'At a constant rate, because the person walks at a constant speed' earns nothing: a constant dx/dt does not make dS/dt constant when S is not a linear function of x. 'Faster, because the shadow is getting smaller' confuses S with dS/dt.

parts.q: Find dS/dx when x = 8, and interpret it with units. If the person walked toward the wall at 3 meters per second instead, which of dS/dx and dS/dt at x = 8 would change, and how? Explain.
parts.a: dS/dx = −40/x² = −40/64 = −0.625 meter of shadow height per meter walked: near x = 8, each meter the person walks toward the wall lowers the shadow by about 0.625 meter (1 point). At 3 meters per second, dS/dx stays −0.625, because it depends only on the geometry of the light, the person and the wall; dS/dt = (dS/dx)(dx/dt) doubles to −1.875 meters per second, because the same drop per meter now happens in half the time (1 point).
parts.n: 'Both double' earns nothing for the second point: dS/dx is a rate per meter walked and does not depend on the walking speed. Giving dS/dx in meters per second earns no interpretation point.

fr.title: A cyclist from a table: a value the data force, a second-order limit and kinetic energy
fr.stem:
A cyclist rides along a straight road. Her position s(t), in meters from a marker, and her velocity v(t), in meters per second, are recorded at selected times t, in seconds. The function s is twice differentiable, and its second derivative, the acceleration a(t) = v′(t), is continuous. At t = 6, the acceleration is a(6) = −0.6 meter per second per second.
t (seconds) · s(t) (meters) · v(t) (meters per second)
0 · 0 · 2.0
2 · 8.1 · 5.8
4 · 21.9 · 7.6
6 · 37.2 · 7.4
8 · 50.1 · 5.2
10 · 56.7 · 1.0
A calculator is not allowed.

parts.q: Must there be a time t, for 2 < t < 8, at which v(t) = 7? Justify your answer.
parts.a: Yes. Because v is differentiable (v′ = a exists), v is continuous on [2, 4] (1 point for the hypothesis on a suitable interval). Since v(2) = 5.8 < 7 < 7.6 = v(4), the Intermediate Value Theorem guarantees a time t with 2 < t < 4, and so 2 < t < 8, at which v(t) = 7 (1 point).
parts.n: Using the endpoints of [2, 8], where v(2) = 5.8 and v(8) = 5.2, and answering 'No, 7 is not between them' earns nothing: the IVT gives no information on that interval, and a smaller interval settles the question. Citing the IVT without stating that v is continuous earns only the second point.

parts.q: Find $\lim_{t \to 6} \frac{s(t) - 37.2 - 7.4(t - 6)}{(t - 6)^{2}}$. Justify each use of L'Hospital's Rule.
parts.a: As t → 6, the numerator → s(6) − 37.2 − 0 = 0 because s is continuous, and the denominator → 0, so the form is 0/0 and L'Hospital's Rule gives $\lim_{t \to 6} \frac{v(t) - 7.4}{2(t - 6)}$ (1 point). The numerator → v(6) − 7.4 = 0 because v is continuous, and the denominator → 0, so the form is 0/0 again (1 point). A second use gives $\lim_{t \to 6} \frac{a(t)}{2} = \frac{a(6)}{2} = -0.3$, using the continuity of a (1 point). (Also acceptable for the last step: the limit of (v(t) − v(6))/(2(t − 6)) is v′(6)/2 by the definition of the derivative.)
parts.n: −0.3 with no check that both limits are 0 at each stage earns only the last point. Writing '= 0/0' as if it were a value, or stopping at the first quotient and substituting to get 0/0, earns no further points.

parts.q: Let L(t) = 37.2 + 7.4(t − 6), the line tangent to the graph of s at t = 6. Use your answer to part (b) to explain why L(t) > s(t) for all t close to 6 with t ≠ 6. What does this say about using L(6.2) to approximate s(6.2)?
parts.a: The quotient in part (b) is [s(t) − L(t)]/(t − 6)², and it approaches −0.3 < 0. So for t close enough to 6 (t ≠ 6) the quotient is negative, and since (t − 6)² > 0 the numerator s(t) − L(t) is negative: L(t) > s(t) (1 point). So L(6.2) = 37.2 + 7.4(0.2) = 38.68 overestimates s(6.2), provided 6.2 is close enough to 6; this is the same conclusion that a(6) < 0 (concave down near t = 6) gives (1 point).
parts.n: 'Overestimate because the cyclist is slowing down' with no link to the limit earns nothing here: the question asks for the reason from part (b). Saying the numerator is negative because the limit is negative, without the positive denominator, earns only the second point.

parts.q: The cyclist and her bicycle have a combined mass of 80 kilograms, so her kinetic energy is K = 40v² joules. Is her kinetic energy increasing or decreasing at t = 6? Find the rate, with units.
parts.a: By the chain rule, dK/dt = 80v(dv/dt) = 80v(t)a(t) (1 point). At t = 6: dK/dt = 80(7.4)(−0.6) = −355.2 joules per second, so her kinetic energy is decreasing at 355.2 joules per second (355.2 watts) (1 point). The velocity is positive and the acceleration negative, so she is slowing down, which agrees.
parts.n: dK/dt = 80v = 592, which forgets the factor dv/dt, earns nothing. A rate 'of 355.2 joules' without 'per second' loses the second point.

u7.intro: Multiple-choice questions 17-24 and free-response question 1 allow a graphing calculator; all other questions are no calculator.

mc.stem:
Questions 1-2 refer to the following.

A slope field for the differential equation dy/dx = F(x, y) has segments at the sixteen points with x = −1, 0, 1, 2 and y = −1, 0, 1, 2. The slope of the segment at each point is given in the table.
y · slope at x = −1 · slope at x = 0 · slope at x = 1 · slope at x = 2
2 · 9 · 6 · 3 · 0
1 · 4 · 2 · 0 · −2
0 · 1 · 0 · −1 · −2
−1 · 0 · 0 · 0 · 0

parts.q:
Which of the following could be F(x, y)?
(A) (x − y)(y + 1)
(B) (y − x³)(y + 1)
(C) y² − x²
(D) (y − x)(y + 1)
parts.a: (D). Check every column, not just the zeros. (y − x)(y + 1) gives, for y = 2: 3(2 − x) = 9, 6, 3, 0; for y = 1: 2(1 − x) = 4, 2, 0, −2; for y = 0: −x = 1, 0, −1, −2; for y = −1: 0 in every column. That is the whole table. (A) has the same zeros (along y = x and y = −1) but the opposite sign everywhere else: at (−1, 2) it gives −9. (B) agrees with the table in the columns x = −1, 0 and 1 (there x³ = x), which is why a student who checks only a few points picks it; at x = 2 it gives (2 − 8)(3) = −18 at (2, 2), where the table shows 0. (C) is 0 along y = x, like the table, but at (−1, 2) it gives 4 − 1 = 3, not 9, and at (0, −1) it gives 1, not 0.
parts.n: FUN-7.C.1, FUN-7.C.2 (topic 7.3); skill 2.C. Thinking: test each candidate against the whole table, including the rows and columns where the slopes are not 0. Trap: (B), which fits three of the four columns.

parts.q:
A student looks at the table and says, "The segments at (−1, −1), (0, 0), (1, 1) and (2, 2) are all horizontal, so the line y = x is a solution curve of this differential equation." Which of the following best evaluates the student's claim?
(A) It is correct, because every point of the line y = x has slope 0, so the line satisfies dy/dx = F(x, y) at each of its points.
(B) It is wrong, because the line y = x has slope 1 while the segments at its points are horizontal; the line y = −1 does match its segments.
(C) It is wrong, because a solution curve can have a horizontal tangent at no more than one of its points.
(D) It is correct, because a line of horizontal segments marks an equilibrium, and a solution that starts on an equilibrium stays on it forever.
parts.a: (B). A curve is a solution when its own slope at each point equals the slope the differential equation assigns there. The line y = x has slope 1 everywhere, but the table assigns slope 0 at each of its points, so dy/dx = 1 ≠ 0 = F(x, x): not a solution. Along y = −1 the segments are also horizontal, and that line is itself horizontal, so y = −1 is a solution (an equilibrium). (A) confuses the slope the equation assigns at the points of a line with the slope of the line. (C) is false: a solution can have slope 0 at many points (y = −1 has slope 0 at every point). (D) applies the idea of an equilibrium to a slanted line; only a horizontal line of zero slopes, y = c, is an equilibrium solution.
parts.n: FUN-7.B.1, FUN-7.C.3 (topics 7.2, 7.4); skill 3.G. Thinking: compare the slope of the proposed curve with the slopes the field assigns along it. Trap: (A), reading 'slope 0 at every point of the line' as 'the line satisfies the equation'.

mc.stem:
Questions 3-5 refer to the following.

Let y = f(x) be the particular solution to the differential equation dy/dx = 1 + xy with the initial condition f(0) = 2. A student uses Euler's method, starting at x = 0 with two steps of equal size, to approximate f(1). The student's work is shown.
Line 1: At (0, 2), dy/dx = 1 + (0)(2) = 1.
Line 2: f(0.5) ≈ 2 + (1)(0.5) = 2.5.
Line 3: At (1, 2.5), dy/dx = 1 + (1)(2.5) = 3.5.
Line 4: f(1) ≈ 2.5 + (3.5)(0.5) = 4.25.

parts.q:
Which of the following identifies the first error in the student's work and its effect on the approximation?
(A) Line 2: the first step should use the slope at x = 0.5 instead of the slope at x = 0, so 2.5 is too small.
(B) Line 3: the slope should be taken at (0.5, 2), keeping the starting y-value 2, which gives an approximation of 3.5.
(C) Line 3: the slope should be taken at (0.5, 2.5), where it is 2.25, so the student's value of 4.25 is too large.
(D) No line is wrong; 4.25 differs from f(1) only because Euler's method gives an approximation, not an exact value.
parts.a: (C). Each Euler step uses the slope at the point where that step starts. The second step starts at (0.5, 2.5), where dy/dx = 1 + (0.5)(2.5) = 2.25, so f(1) ≈ 2.5 + (2.25)(0.5) = 3.625. The student evaluated the slope at (1, 2.5), the x-value where the step ends; that slope, 3.5, is larger, so the student's 4.25 is too large compared with the correct Euler value 3.625. (A) describes the same mistake the student made in Line 3, but moved to Line 2; Line 2 is correct, since the first step starts at (0, 2). (B) moves x forward but keeps the starting y-value; the second step starts at the point the first step reached, (0.5, 2.5), not at (0.5, 2). (D) treats the error as the method's normal error; the method itself fixes where each slope is taken, and Line 3 breaks that rule.
parts.n: FUN-7.C.4 (topic 7.5, BC only); skill 3.G. Thinking: check each line against the rule that a step uses the slope at its starting point, then compare the results. Trap: (D), which accepts any slope as 'part of the approximation'.

parts.q:
Suppose Line 3 and Line 4 are corrected. How does the corrected two-step Euler approximation compare with f(1)?
(A) It is less than f(1), because d²y/dx² = y + x + x²y > 0 for x ≥ 0 and y > 0, so the curve lies above its tangent segments.
(B) It is greater than f(1), because d²y/dx² > 0 on the interval, so each tangent segment lies above the solution curve.
(C) It is less than f(1), because dy/dx > 0 on the interval, and tangent segments always lie below an increasing curve.
(D) It is within 0.01 of f(1), because two steps of size 0.5 are enough to follow the curve closely on so short an interval.
parts.a: (A). Differentiate implicitly: d²y/dx² = y + x·dy/dx = y + x(1 + xy) = y + x + x²y. The solution starts at y = 2, and while x ≥ 0 and y > 0, dy/dx = 1 + xy > 0, so y stays positive and d²y/dx² > 0: the solution curve is concave up on 0 ≤ x ≤ 1. Each Euler segment follows a tangent direction, and a concave-up curve lies above its tangent lines, so the approximation (3.625) is less than f(1) (about 4.708). (B) has the concavity right but the geometry backwards: tangent lines lie below a concave-up curve. (C) reaches the right verdict for the wrong reason: being increasing says nothing about which side of the tangent line the curve is on (a concave-down increasing curve lies below its tangents). (D) assumes two steps on a short interval give a small error; here the error is more than 1, because the slope grows quickly along the curve.
parts.n: FUN-7.C.4 (topic 7.5, BC only), with implicit differentiation from unit 3; skill 1.F. Thinking: find the sign of d²y/dx² along the solution and turn concavity into over or under. Trap: (C), increasing mistaken for concave up.

parts.q:
Suppose the student had used four steps of size 0.25 instead, with every slope taken correctly. How would that approximation compare with the corrected two-step approximation and with f(1)?
(A) It would be less than the two-step approximation, because four steps add up more error than two steps do.
(B) It would be greater than f(1), because shorter steps overshoot a solution curve that is concave up.
(C) It would equal the two-step approximation, because both approximations begin with the same slope of 1 at (0, 2).
(D) It would be between the two-step approximation and f(1), because shorter steps stay closer to the concave-up curve.
parts.a: (D). The solution is concave up on 0 ≤ x ≤ 1 (question 4), so every Euler approximation built from tangent segments falls below f(1). Shorter steps update the slope more often; since the slope keeps increasing along the curve, the four-step path rises faster than the two-step path and stays closer to the curve. The four-step value is 4.075, between 3.625 and f(1) ≈ 4.708. (A) treats each step as adding error; in fact each shorter step makes a smaller error, and the total error shrinks. (B) reverses the geometry: tangent segments of a concave-up curve lie below it, so shorter steps approach f(1) from below, never passing it. (C) stops after the first step: the approximations share the first slope, but the four-step version recomputes the slope at x = 0.25, 0.5 and 0.75.
parts.n: FUN-7.C.4 (topic 7.5, BC only); skill 1.F. Thinking: predict how a smaller step size changes an Euler approximation, using the concavity already found. Trap: (A), 'more steps, more error'.

mc.stem:
Questions 6-8 refer to the following.

A biologist estimates the growth rate of a deer population P, in deer, at five population sizes. The biologist believes P follows a logistic model. Time t is measured in years.
P (deer) · dP/dt (deer per year)
200 · 36
500 · 75
1000 · 100
1500 · 75
1800 · 36
Questions 6-8 are BC only (logistic models).

parts.q:
Which of the following differential equations is consistent with every row of the table?
(A) dP/dt = 0.0001P(2000 − P)
(B) dP/dt = 0.2P(1 − P/1000)
(C) dP/dt = 0.1P(1 − P/2000)
(D) dP/dt = 0.0002P(2000 − P)
parts.a: (A). Test each row: 0.0001(200)(1800) = 36, 0.0001(500)(1500) = 75, 0.0001(1000)(1000) = 100, 0.0001(1500)(500) = 75 and 0.0001(1800)(200) = 36. It is the logistic equation 0.2P(1 − P/2000) written in the form kP(L − P): the rates are symmetric about P = 1000 = L/2, so L = 2000, and the greatest rate kL/4 = 100 gives k = 0.2. (B) takes the P-value of the fastest growth, 1000, as the carrying capacity; then dP/dt would be 0 at P = 1000, not 100. (C) solves 100 = k(1000) and forgets the factor 1 − 1000/2000 = 1/2; it gives 50 at P = 1000. (D) converts 0.2P(1 − P/2000) by dividing 0.2 by 1000 instead of 2000; it gives 200 at P = 1000, double every rate in the table.
parts.n: FUN-7.H.1, FUN-7.H.2 (topic 7.9, BC only); skill 2.C. Thinking: read L from the symmetry of the rates and k from the peak, then match an equation written in another form. Trap: (B), the peak mistaken for the carrying capacity.

parts.q:
The same differential equation models a second herd, but this herd starts with P(0) = 2400 deer. Which of the following describes P for t ≥ 0?
(A) P decreases toward 1000, because the table shows that the population changes fastest at P = 1000.
(B) P increases without bound, because every growth rate in the table is positive, so P never decreases.
(C) P decreases toward 2000 with a concave-up graph, because dP/dt < 0 and |dP/dt| shrinks as P nears 2000.
(D) P decreases toward 2000 with a concave-down graph, because dP/dt < 0, so the graph of P bends downward.
parts.a: (C). For P > 2000, dP/dt = 0.0001P(2000 − P) < 0, so P decreases; it cannot pass the equilibrium P = 2000, so it approaches 2000. As P falls toward 2000, the factor 2000 − P shrinks toward 0, so the rate of decrease shrinks: P decreases more and more slowly, which is a concave-up graph. (In symbols, d²P/dt² = 0.0001(2000 − 2P)·dP/dt, a product of two negatives when P > 2000.) (A) treats the P-value of fastest change as a limit; the only nonzero equilibrium is 2000. (B) extends the table beyond its range: the table stops at 1800, and above 2000 the rates are negative. (D) confuses decreasing with concave down; a quantity that decreases ever more slowly has a concave-up graph.
parts.n: FUN-7.H.2, FUN-7.H.3 (topic 7.9, BC only); skill 3.F. Thinking: predict the long-run value and the concavity from the sign and size of dP/dt above the carrying capacity. Trap: (D), 'decreasing, so concave down'.

parts.q:
For the first herd, P = 1000 at a certain moment. The biologist estimates how long the herd will take to grow from 1000 to 1100 deer: 100 deer ÷ 100 deer per year = 1 year. Which of the following best evaluates this estimate?
(A) It is too long, because once P passes 1000 the herd grows faster than 100 deer per year.
(B) It is too short, because dP/dt < 100 for 1000 < P < 1100, so the herd needs more than 1 year.
(C) It is exact, because a logistic population grows at a constant rate near its inflection point.
(D) It is too long, because the graph of P is concave up for P > 1000, so P rises above its tangent line.
parts.a: (B). The rate 100 deer per year at P = 1000 is the greatest rate the model allows (the rates are symmetric about 1000 and fall off on both sides). For every P between 1000 and 1100 the herd grows more slowly than 100 deer per year, so gaining 100 deer takes longer than 1 year. (Solving the model gives 5 ln(11/9) ≈ 1.003 years, just over 1.) (A) has the rates rising after 1000; the table shows them falling (75 at P = 1500). (C) turns 'the rate is greatest at the inflection point' into 'the rate is constant there'; the rate stops increasing at P = 1000 but immediately starts decreasing. (D) has the concavity backwards: for P > 1000 the rate decreases, so the graph of P is concave down and lies below its tangent line.
parts.n: FUN-7.H.2, FUN-7.H.4 (topic 7.9, BC only); skill 1.F. Thinking: use the fact that 100 is the maximum rate to decide whether a rate-based estimate of time is too long or too short. Trap: (C), the inflection point read as a constant rate.

mc.stem:
Questions 9-10 refer to the following.

A student is asked to find the particular solution of the differential equation $\frac{dy}{dx} = \frac{\cos x}{2y}$ with the initial condition y(0) = −1. The student's work is shown.
Step 1: 2y dy = cos x dx
Step 2: y² = sin x + C
Step 3: (−1)² = sin 0 + C, so C = 1
Step 4: y = √(1 + sin x)

parts.q:
Which of the following best evaluates the student's work?
(A) Step 1 is wrong: the variables separate as dy/(2y) = cos x dx, so every later step inherits the error.
(B) Step 2 is wrong: each side needs its own constant, so one initial condition cannot determine both of them.
(C) Step 3 is wrong: the initial condition may be used only after the equation has been solved for y.
(D) Step 4 is wrong: √(1 + sin x) satisfies the differential equation, but its value at x = 0 is 1, not −1.
parts.a: (D). Steps 1 to 3 are correct: multiplying both sides by 2y dx gives 2y dy = cos x dx, the antiderivatives are y² and sin x plus one constant, and y = −1 at x = 0 gives C = 1. Then y² = 1 + sin x has two square roots, and the initial condition picks the sign: y must be −1 at x = 0, so y = −√(1 + sin x). The student's positive root does satisfy dy/dx = cos x/(2y), but it passes through (0, 1), so it is the wrong particular solution. (A) divides by 2y on the wrong side; from dy/dx = cos x/(2y), the 2y multiplies dy. (B) is a common worry, but two constants C₁ and C₂ always combine into the single constant C = C₂ − C₁. (C) reverses good practice: substituting the initial condition before solving for y is allowed, and it is often the easiest way to find C.
parts.n: FUN-7.D.1, FUN-7.E.1 (topics 7.6, 7.7); skill 3.G. Thinking: check each step, and use the initial condition to choose the branch of a square root. Trap: (B), the 'two constants' worry.

parts.q:
What is the domain of the correct particular solution?
(A) All real numbers
(B) −π/2 < x < 3π/2
(C) −π/2 < x < π/2
(D) −π/2 ≤ x ≤ 3π/2
parts.a: (B). The particular solution is y = −√(1 + sin x). The differential equation divides by 2y, so y cannot be 0, and y = 0 exactly where sin x = −1, at x = −π/2 + 2πk. A particular solution is defined on one open interval that contains the initial x-value 0 and avoids those points: −π/2 < x < 3π/2. (A) ignores the points where y = 0 and dy/dx = cos x/(2y) is undefined. (C) stops at x = π/2, where cos x changes sign; the slope is 0 there but the solution is still defined, since y = −√2 ≠ 0. (D) includes the endpoints, where y = 0; there cos x/(2y) is undefined, so the differential equation cannot hold at those points.
parts.n: FUN-7.E.3 (topic 7.7); skill 3.G. Thinking: find where the particular solution or the differential equation breaks down, then keep the one interval containing the initial point. Trap: (D), the closed interval.

mc.stem:
Questions 11-12 refer to the following.

Water drains from a tank through a small hole in its bottom. Let h(t) be the depth of the water, in centimeters, t minutes after the draining starts. The depth decreases at a rate proportional to the square root of the depth. At t = 0 the depth is 16 centimeters, and at that moment the depth is decreasing at 2 centimeters per minute.

parts.q:
Which of the following differential equations models the depth of the water?
(A) dh/dt = −2√h
(B) dh/dt = −h/8
(C) dh/dt = −(1/2)√h
(D) dh/dt = −(1/8)√h
parts.a: (C). 'Decreases at a rate proportional to the square root of the depth' means dh/dt = −k√h with k > 0. At h = 16, dh/dt = −2, so −2 = −k·√16 = −4k and k = 1/2. (A) uses the given rate, 2, as the constant of proportionality; it would make the depth fall at 8 centimeters per minute when h = 16. (B) makes the rate proportional to h itself (2 = k·16 gives k = 1/8), which is exponential decay, not the stated model. (D) has the square root in the equation but finds k by dividing 2 by 16 instead of by √16 = 4; it gives a rate of 0.5 centimeter per minute at h = 16.
parts.n: FUN-7.A.1 (topic 7.1); skill 2.C. Thinking: translate 'proportional to the square root' into an equation, then use the given rate to find the constant. Trap: (D), dividing by h instead of √h.

parts.q:
A student says, "As the tank drains, h gets smaller, so dh/dt gets closer to 0. Just like exponential decay, the depth approaches 0 but the tank never empties." Which of the following best evaluates the student's claim?
(A) It is wrong: separating variables gives √h = 4 − t/4, so the tank is empty at t = 16 minutes.
(B) It is correct: since dh/dt → 0 as h → 0, the depth can only approach 0 as t increases without bound.
(C) It is wrong: the depth falls at 2 centimeters per minute, so the tank is empty at t = 8 minutes.
(D) It is wrong: separating variables gives √h = 4 − t/2, so the tank is empty at t = 8 minutes.
parts.a: (A). Separate: $h^{-1/2}$ dh = −(1/2) dt, so 2√h = −t/2 + C. At t = 0, 2√16 = 8 = C, so √h = 4 − t/4, and h = (4 − t/4)² for 0 ≤ t ≤ 16. The depth reaches 0 at t = 16 minutes. The rate does shrink as h shrinks, but √h shrinks much more slowly than h near 0, so, unlike exponential decay, the depth reaches 0 in a finite time. (B) is the student's analogy with dh/dt = −kh; a rate that tends to 0 does not by itself stop the depth from reaching 0. (C) treats the rate at t = 0 as constant; the rate slows as the tank drains, so emptying takes longer than 8 minutes. (D) drops the factor 2 from the antiderivative of $h^{-1/2}$, which is 2√h, not √h.
parts.n: FUN-7.D.1, FUN-7.D.2 (topic 7.6), contrasted with FUN-7.F.2 (topic 7.8); skill 3.G. Thinking: solve the model to test a claim made by analogy with exponential decay. Trap: (B), the analogy itself.

parts.q:
The table gives selected values of a differentiable function f and its derivative f′.
x · f(x) · f′(x)
0 · 2 · 1
1 · 3 · 2
2 · 5 · 4
A student notices that f′(x) = f(x) − 1 in every row and concludes that f is a solution of the differential equation dy/dx = y − 1 on 0 ≤ x ≤ 2. Which of the following best evaluates the student's conclusion?
(A) It is correct, because the equation f′(x) = f(x) − 1 holds at every value of x listed in the table.
(B) It is correct, because Euler's method for dy/dx = y − 1 from (0, 2) with step size 1 gives exactly 3 and 5.
(C) It is wrong: the only solution through (0, 2) is y = 1 + eˣ, and 1 + e ≠ 3, so f cannot be a solution.
(D) It cannot be decided: values at three points can neither confirm nor rule out that f is a solution.
parts.a: (C). Separating dy/dx = y − 1 gives ln|y − 1| = x + C; with y = 2 at x = 0, the particular solution is y = 1 + eˣ, and there is only one solution through (0, 2). That solution has y(1) = 1 + e ≈ 3.72, but f(1) = 3, so f is not a solution, even though it agrees with the equation at the three listed points. (A) verifies an equation at a few points; a solution must satisfy it at every x in the interval. (B) notices, correctly, that the table is exactly the Euler polygon with step size 1, but Euler's method gives approximations of the solution, not its values. (D) is half right: three points cannot confirm a solution, but they can rule one out, because the initial condition fixes the unique solution and its value at x = 1 does not match.
parts.n: FUN-7.B.1, FUN-7.E.1 (topics 7.2, 7.7); skill 3.G. Thinking: use the unique particular solution through (0, 2) to test data that agree with the equation pointwise. Trap: (B), the table that happens to match Euler's method.

parts.q:
Two models are proposed for a population P, with t measured in years and P(0) = 100 in both.
Model I: dP/dt = 0.3P
Model II: dP/dt = 0.3P(1 − P/600)
Which of the following correctly compares the two models? (Model II is logistic, which is BC only.)
(A) Both grow at 30 per year at t = 0, because both have k = 0.3, and the models separate only later.
(B) Model II grows at 25 per year at t = 0, and its population stays below Model I's for all t > 0.
(C) Model II eventually overtakes Model I, because Model II's population grows fastest when P = 300.
(D) The models agree closely for all t > 0, because the factor 1 − P/600 stays close to 1.
parts.a: (B). At t = 0, Model I gives 0.3(100) = 30 per year and Model II gives 0.3(100)(1 − 100/600) = 25 per year. For any positive P below 600, Model II's rate is smaller than Model I's rate at the same population, so Model II starts slower and can never catch up: its population stays below Model I's for every t > 0. (Model II levels off toward 600 while Model I grows without bound.) (A) reads k as the whole growth rate; in Model II the rate is 0.3P times a factor less than 1. (C) confuses fastest growth with faster than the other model; at P = 300 Model II grows at 45 per year, while Model I, already larger, grows faster still. (D) is true only while P is small compared with 600; as P nears 600 the factor nears 0.
parts.n: FUN-7.F.2 (topic 7.8) and FUN-7.H.1, FUN-7.H.2 (topic 7.9, BC only); skill 2.E. Thinking: compare the two rates at the same population, then turn that into a comparison of the populations. Trap: (A), same k, same rate.

mc.stem:
Questions 15-16 refer to the following.

Consider the differential equation dy/dx = x − y + 1, which is not separable. Let y = f(x) be the particular solution with f(0) = 2. In the slope field for this equation, every segment along the line y = x + 1 is horizontal.

parts.q:
Which of the following describes the graph of f for x > 0?
(A) It stays above the line y = x and approaches it, because u = f(x) − x satisfies du/dx = −u.
(B) It levels off at a horizontal asymptote, because the slopes are 0 along the line y = x + 1.
(C) It crosses the line y = x and then stays below it, because every slope above that line is less than 1.
(D) It stays a vertical distance 2 above the line y = x, because the solution curves are lines y = x + C.
parts.a: (A). The line y = x is itself a solution: its slope is 1, and x − x + 1 = 1. Let u = f(x) − x, the vertical distance above that line. Then du/dx = f′(x) − 1 = (x − f(x) + 1) − 1 = −u, so u = u(0)e⁻ˣ = 2e⁻ˣ. The distance is always positive and shrinks to 0: f(x) = x + 2e⁻ˣ stays above y = x and approaches it. (B) treats the line of horizontal segments as an equilibrium; y = x + 1 is not horizontal, so it is not a solution, and f passes through it. (C) is right that slopes above y = x are less than 1, which is why f bends toward the line, but the gap decays exponentially and never reaches 0. (D) guesses that the solutions are parallel lines; y = x + 2 has slope 1, but the equation gives x − (x + 2) + 1 = −1 along it, so it is not a solution.
parts.n: FUN-7.C.2, FUN-7.C.3 (topic 7.4), with FUN-7.D.1 (topic 7.6); skill 2.E. Thinking: find a line that is a solution, then study the distance from it, which satisfies a separable equation. Trap: (B), an isocline mistaken for an asymptote.

parts.q:
A student claims: "f has a relative minimum at the point where its graph meets the line y = x + 1, because dy/dx = 0 there." Which of the following best evaluates the claim?
(A) The claim is wrong: the graph of f never meets the line y = x + 1, because f stays above that line for all x.
(B) The claim is right and complete: a solution curve has a relative minimum at each point where its slope is 0.
(C) The conclusion is right, and the reason is that d²y/dx² = 1 everywhere, so every solution curve is concave up.
(D) The conclusion is right, but dy/dx = 0 is not enough: where dy/dx = 0, d²y/dx² = 1 − dy/dx = 1 > 0.
parts.a: (D). A zero slope only locates a candidate. Differentiating the equation, d²y/dx² = 1 − dy/dx, so at any point where dy/dx = 0 the second derivative is 1 > 0, and the Second Derivative Test gives a relative minimum. (The graph does meet the line: f(x) = x + 2e⁻ˣ equals x + 1 when x = ln 2.) (A) is false: f(0) = 2 lies above y = x + 1, but the gap f(x) − (x + 1) = 2e⁻ˣ − 1 is 0 at x = ln 2. (B) treats every horizontal tangent as a minimum; a zero slope could also be a maximum or neither, so a test is needed. (C) differentiates x − y + 1 as if y were a constant; y depends on x, so d²y/dx² = 1 − dy/dx, which equals 1 only where dy/dx = 0.
parts.n: FUN-7.C.2 (topic 7.4); skill 3.D. Thinking: find d²y/dx² from the differential equation and apply the Second Derivative Test at every point with dy/dx = 0 at once. Trap: (C), which gets 1 by treating y as a constant.

mc.stem:
Questions 17-18 refer to the following.

A bacteria culture grows at a rate proportional to its size, so the number of bacteria P(t) satisfies dP/dt = kP, where t is measured in hours. The culture has 1200 bacteria at t = 0 and 1750 bacteria at t = 3. A graphing calculator is allowed.

parts.q:
According to the model, at what time t will the culture reach 5000 bacteria?
(A) 8.348 hours
(B) 9.341 hours
(C) 11.348 hours
(D) 20.727 hours
parts.a: (C). The solution is $P = 1200e^{kt}$. From P(3) = 1750, $e^{3k} = \frac{1750}{1200}$, so k = ln(1750/1200)/3 ≈ 0.12576. Then $1200e^{kt} = 5000$ gives t = ln(5000/1200)/k ≈ 11.348 hours. (A) measures the time from t = 3, starting at 1750 with ln(5000/1750)/k; that is the time after the second count, not after t = 0. (B) uses the percent increase per hour, 550/(1200·3) ≈ 0.15278, as k; k is a continuous rate, ln(1750/1200)/3, which is smaller. (D) assumes a constant rate of 550/3 bacteria per hour, a linear model, which ignores that the rate grows with P.
parts.n: FUN-7.G.1, FUN-7.F.2 (topic 7.8); skill 1.E. Thinking: build $y = y_{0}e^{kt}$ from two data points and solve for a time, with a calculator. Trap: (B), the percent change used as k.

parts.q:
At t = 6 the culture is counted again and has 2400 bacteria. Which conclusion does this count support?
(A) The model predicts about 2552 at t = 6, more than the count, so the relative growth rate fell after t = 3.
(B) The model predicts about 2300 at t = 6, less than the count, so the culture grew faster than the model.
(C) The count confirms the model, because the culture doubled in 6 hours, and doubling time is constant.
(D) The model predicts about 2552 at t = 6, so the value of k must have increased after t = 3 to explain the gap.
parts.a: (A). The exponential model predicts P(6) = 1200(1750/1200)² ≈ 2552, but the culture has only 2400. Over 3 ≤ t ≤ 6 the growth corresponds to k = ln(2400/1750)/3 ≈ 0.105, less than the 0.126 of the first 3 hours: the relative growth rate (1/P)(dP/dt) fell, which is what a culture approaching a limit, as in a logistic model, would show. (B) predicts with a constant 550 bacteria per 3 hours (1200 + 2·550 = 2300), a linear model, not the exponential one. (C) checks a single doubling; the model's own prediction for t = 6 is 2552, and a constant doubling time is exactly what the data contradict (the first 3 hours multiplied P by 1.458, the next 3 by only 1.371). (D) reverses the effect of k: a larger k would make the culture grow faster and overshoot 2552, not fall short of it.
parts.n: FUN-7.G.1, FUN-7.F.2 (topic 7.8); skill 3.G. Thinking: test a model's prediction against new data and say what the mismatch means about k. Trap: (C), one doubling taken as confirmation.

mc.stem:
Questions 19-20 refer to the following.

Let y = f(x) be the particular solution to the differential equation dy/dx = √x·cos x, for x ≥ 0, with the initial condition f(1) = 3. The solution cannot be written with elementary functions, so its values must be found from a definite integral. A graphing calculator is allowed.

parts.q:
What is the minimum value of f on the interval 0 ≤ x ≤ 5?
(A) −3.350
(B) −0.350
(C) −0.259
(D) 2.469
parts.a: (B). By the Fundamental Theorem of Calculus, $f(x) = 3 + \int_{1}^{x} \sqrt{t}\cos t\,dt$. On (0, 5), f′(x) = √x·cos x = 0 only at x = π/2 and x = 3π/2, and f′ changes from negative to positive at 3π/2. Compare the candidates: f(0) ≈ 2.469, f(π/2) ≈ 3.173, f(3π/2) ≈ −0.350 and f(5) ≈ −0.259. The minimum is −0.350, at x = 3π/2. (A) is $\int_{1}^{3\pi/2} \sqrt{t}\cos t\,dt$ alone; it leaves out the initial value 3. (C) is f(5), the value at the right endpoint; f rises from x = 3π/2 to x = 5, so the endpoint is not the lowest point. (D) is f(0), the value at the left endpoint; f increases from there at first, but it later falls much lower.
parts.n: FUN-7.E.2 (topic 7.7), with the Candidates Test from unit 5; skill 1.E. Thinking: write the particular solution as an initial value plus an integral, then compare the critical points with the endpoints. Trap: (A), the integral without the initial value.

parts.q:
A student uses the line tangent to the graph of f at x = 4 to approximate f(4.5), and says the approximation is too large because f is decreasing at x = 4. Which of the following best evaluates the student's work?
(A) The approximation is −0.503, and it is too large, as the student says, because a tangent line always lies above a decreasing graph.
(B) The approximation is −0.503, and it is too large, because f″(4) < 0, so near x = 4 the graph lies below its tangent line.
(C) The approximation is −0.503, and it is too small, because f′(4) < 0 and a line with negative slope lies below the graph.
(D) The approximation is −0.503, and it is too small, because f″(x) > 0 on 4 ≤ x ≤ 4.5, so the graph lies above its tangent line.
parts.a: (D). The tangent line gives f(4) + f′(4)(0.5) = 0.150 + (2cos 4)(0.5) ≈ 0.150 − 0.654 = −0.503. Whether it is too large or too small depends on concavity, not on whether f is decreasing: f″(x) = cos x/(2√x) − √x·sin x, which is positive on 4 ≤ x ≤ 4.5 (there sin x < 0, and the second term outweighs the first; f″(4) ≈ 1.350). The graph is concave up and lies above its tangent line, so −0.503 is too small; indeed f(4.5) ≈ −0.302. (A) is the student's reasoning: the sign of f′ does not decide which side of the tangent line the graph is on. (B) gets f″(4) < 0 by treating sin 4 as positive; 4 radians is between π and 2π, where sine is negative. (C) has the right verdict for a wrong reason: a line with negative slope can lie above a graph that is concave down.
parts.n: FUN-7.E.2 (topic 7.7), with tangent-line approximation from unit 4; skill 1.F. Thinking: decide over or under from the sign of f″ on the whole interval, computed from the differential equation. Trap: (B), sin 4 taken as positive.

parts.q:
A pot of soup is taken off the stove at 100°C at an unknown time and left in a kitchen kept at 20°C. Its temperature T, in degrees Celsius, satisfies dT/dt = −k(T − 20) for a positive constant k, where t is measured in hours. At 1:00 p.m. the soup is at 64°C, and at 1:30 p.m. it is at 52°C. About how long before 1:00 p.m. was the soup taken off the stove?
(A) 0.939 hours
(B) 1.075 hours
(C) 1.500 hours
(D) 1.877 hours
parts.a: (A). Let t = 0 at 1:00 p.m. The solution is $T - 20 = 44e^{-kt}$, since T − 20 = 44 at t = 0. At t = 0.5, 32 = $44e^{-0.5k}$, so k = 2 ln(44/32) ≈ 0.6369 per hour. The soup was at 100°C when $80 = 44e^{-kt}$, so t = −ln(80/44)/k ≈ −0.939: about 0.939 hours before 1:00 p.m. (B) leaves out the room temperature, fitting T = $T_{0}e^{-kt}$ to 64 and 52 and solving for 100; the model says the difference T − 20 decays exponentially, not T. (C) assumes the soup cools at a constant 24 degrees per hour; it cools faster when it is hotter, so it took less time to fall from 100 to 64. (D) finds k = ln(44/32) from the two readings but forgets that they are half an hour apart, so the answer comes out in half-hours.
parts.n: FUN-7.F.1, FUN-7.G.1 (topic 7.8), with FUN-7.A.1 (topic 7.1); skill 1.E. Thinking: turn Newton's law into an exponential model for T − 20, fit it to two readings and run it backward. Trap: (B), decaying T instead of T − 20.

parts.q:
In a school of 1200 students, the number of students who have heard a rumor t days after it starts is y(t), where dy/dt = 0.9y(1 − y/1200) and y(0) = 20. The solution is $y(t) = \frac{1200}{1 + 59e^{-0.9t}}$. At t = 3 days, how fast is the rumor spreading, and is that rate increasing or decreasing?
(A) About 218 students per day, and increasing, because the rate 0.9y is still growing.
(B) About 174 students per day, and decreasing, because fewer students are left to hear it.
(C) About 270 students per day, and at its greatest, because the greatest rate is kL/4 = 270.
(D) About 174 students per day, and increasing, because y(3) is less than 600, half the school.
parts.a: (D). y(3) = 1200/(1 + $59e^{-2.7}$) ≈ 241.69, so dy/dt = 0.9(241.69)(1 − 241.69/1200) ≈ 173.71, about 174 students per day. The rate 0.9y(1 − y/1200) increases with y while y < 600 (in symbols, d²y/dt² = 0.9(1 − y/600)·dy/dt > 0), and y(3) < 600, so the rate is still increasing. (A) drops the factor 1 − y/1200 and computes 0.9y ≈ 217.5, the rate of unlimited exponential growth; the verdict 'increasing' is right, but the rate is not. (B) sees only one factor: fewer students remain who have not heard, but more students are spreading it, and the product y(1200 − y) keeps growing until y = 600. (C) gives the greatest rate, kL/4 = 0.9(1200)/4 = 270, which occurs when y = 600, at t = ln 59/0.9 ≈ 4.53 days, not at t = 3.
parts.n: FUN-7.H.2, FUN-7.H.4 (topic 7.9, BC only); skill 3.F. Thinking: evaluate the rate from the model at a computed value of y, then decide from y < L/2 whether the rate is still rising. Trap: (B), which weighs only the students still to hear it.

parts.q:
A tank holds V(t) liters of water at time t minutes. Water flows in at 5 liters per minute and drains out at 0.4√V liters per minute, so dV/dt = 5 − 0.4√V, with V(0) = 100. What is the approximation to V(3) found by Euler's method, starting at t = 0 with three steps of equal size? (Euler's method is BC only.)
(A) 101.980
(B) 102.941
(C) 103.000
(D) 103.883
parts.a: (B). With step size 1: V(1) ≈ 100 + (5 − 0.4√100)(1) = 101; V(2) ≈ 101 + (5 − 0.4√101)(1) ≈ 101.980; V(3) ≈ 101.980 + (5 − 0.4√101.980)(1) ≈ 102.941. Each step recomputes the rate from the volume the previous step reached. (A) stops after two steps; it approximates V(2). (C) uses the starting rate, 1 liter per minute, for all three minutes; that is the tangent line at t = 0, not Euler's method, because the rate is never updated. (D) takes a fourth step, counting the four times t = 0, 1, 2, 3 as four steps; three steps of size 1 end at t = 3.
parts.n: FUN-7.C.4 (topic 7.5, BC only), with FUN-7.A.1 (topic 7.1); skill 1.E. Thinking: carry the rate forward from each new volume, with the calculator for the square roots. Trap: (C), one slope for every step.

parts.q:
A skydiver falls from rest. Her downward velocity v(t), in meters per second, satisfies dv/dt = 9.8 − 0.2v, with v(0) = 0 and t in seconds. How far has she fallen by the time her velocity reaches 90% of its limiting value?
(A) 99.225 meters
(B) 253.860 meters
(C) 343.633 meters
(D) 564.133 meters
parts.a: (C). The limiting velocity is where dv/dt = 0: v = 49 meters per second. Separating variables gives $v = 49(1 - e^{-0.2t})$, and v = 0.9(49) = 44.1 when $e^{-0.2t} = 0.1$, at t = 5 ln 10 ≈ 11.513 seconds. The distance fallen is $\int_{0}^{11.513} 49(1 - e^{-0.2t})\,dt$ ≈ 343.633 meters. (A) ignores the drag term, so v = 9.8t reaches 44.1 at t = 4.5 and the distance is 4.9(4.5)² = 99.225; with drag she needs longer and falls farther. (B) multiplies the average of the first and last velocities, 22.05, by 11.513; that treats v as linear in t, but v rises quickly at first, so it underestimates the distance. (D) uses the limiting velocity, 49, for the whole 11.513 seconds; she moves slower than that the whole time.
parts.n: FUN-7.F.1, FUN-7.G.1 (topic 7.8), with motion from unit 8; skill 1.E. Thinking: solve the model for v, find the time from the limiting value, then integrate velocity for distance. Trap: (B), the average of two velocities.

fr.title: Drug levels from a table: the Mean Value Theorem, an exponential fit and a second dose
fr.stem:
A patient is given a 400-milligram dose of a drug at time t = 0. The amount of the drug in the patient's bloodstream is A(t) milligrams, where t is measured in hours and A is differentiable. Selected values of A(t), measured in a lab, are given in the table.
t (hours) · A(t) (milligrams)
0 · 400
2 · 330
4 · 272
6 · 225
8 · 185
A graphing calculator is allowed.

parts.q: Use the data in the table to approximate A′(4). Show the computations that lead to your answer, and interpret the meaning of your answer in the context of the problem, with units.
parts.a: A′(4) ≈ (A(6) − A(2))/(6 − 2) = (225 − 330)/4 = −26.25 milligrams per hour (1 point). At time t = 4 hours, the amount of the drug in the bloodstream is decreasing at a rate of about 26.25 milligrams per hour (1 point).
parts.n: A quotient from one side of t = 4, such as (225 − 272)/2 = −23.5, also earns the first point. 'The drug goes down by 26.25' with no 'per hour', or with no time t = 4, loses the interpretation point, and so does calling A itself a rate.

parts.q: Must there be a time t, for 2 < t < 6, at which A′(t) = −26.25? Justify your answer.
parts.a: Yes. Because A is differentiable, it is continuous on [2, 6] and differentiable on (2, 6) (1 point for the hypotheses). By the Mean Value Theorem, there is a time c with 2 < c < 6 at which A′(c) = (A(6) − A(2))/(6 − 2) = (225 − 330)/4 = −26.25 (1 point for the conclusion, naming the theorem).
parts.n: 'Yes, by the MVT' with no hypotheses earns only 1 point. Citing the Intermediate Value Theorem earns nothing: nothing says A′ is continuous, and the table gives no values of A′ to compare with −26.25.

parts.q: A pharmacist claims that these data support the model dA/dt = kA for some constant k. Do you agree? Justify your answer using the data in the table.
parts.a: Yes, the data support the model (1 point for a conclusion reached through a correct test). If dA/dt = kA, then $A(t) = 400e^{kt}$, so A(t + 2)/A(t) = $e^{2k}$ must be the same for every 2-hour interval. The ratios are 330/400 = 0.825, 272/330 ≈ 0.824, 225/272 ≈ 0.827 and 185/225 ≈ 0.822, which are nearly constant (1 point). (Also acceptable: the relative rate A′(4)/A(4) ≈ −26.25/272 ≈ −0.097 matches the constant ln(185/400)/8 ≈ −0.096 found from the first and last rows.)
parts.n: 'Yes, because A is decreasing' earns nothing: every decay model is decreasing. The differences 70, 58, 47 and 40 are not constant; that rules out a linear model, but an exponential model needs constant ratios, not constant differences.

parts.q: Assume that A satisfies dA/dt = kA with A(0) = 400 and A(8) = 185. The drug works while A(t) ≥ 100, so the doctor gives a second 400-milligram dose at the moment A falls to 100 milligrams. At what time is the second dose given? After the second dose, how many hours pass before A again falls to 100 milligrams? Explain why this second interval is longer than the first.
parts.a: k = ln(185/400)/8 ≈ −0.09639 per hour (1 point). Then $400e^{kt} = 100$ when t = ln(1/4)/k ≈ 14.382 hours, the time of the second dose (1 point). Just after the second dose A = 100 + 400 = 500, and $500e^{k(t - 14.382)} = 100$ after ln(1/5)/k ≈ 16.697 hours (at t ≈ 31.080). Under exponential decay the time to fall depends only on the ratio of the amounts: the first interval is a fall by a factor of 4 (400 to 100), the second by a factor of 5 (500 to 100), because 100 milligrams remained when the second dose was given, so it lasts longer (1 point).
parts.n: Restarting from 400 instead of 500 gives 14.382 hours again and loses the last point. 'The intervals are equal because the half-life is constant' earns nothing for the explanation: a constant half-life means equal times for equal ratios, and the ratios here differ.

fr.title: Euler's method, a particular solution and a student's maximum value
fr.stem:
Consider the differential equation dy/dx = y(1 − x). Let y = f(x) be the particular solution to this differential equation with the initial condition f(0) = 2.
A calculator is not allowed. Parts (a) and (c) use Euler's method, which is BC only.

parts.q: Use Euler's method, starting at x = 0 with two steps of equal size, to approximate f(1). Show the work that leads to your answer.
parts.n: Using the slope 2 for both steps gives 4 and earns at most the first point; so does a single step of size 1, which also gives 4 but is not two steps.

parts.q: Find y = f(x), the particular solution to the differential equation with the initial condition f(0) = 2.
parts.a: Separate the variables: dy/y = (1 − x) dx (1 point). Antidifferentiate: ln|y| = x − x²/2 + C (1 point). With f(0) = 2, C = ln 2, so ln|y| = x − x²/2 + ln 2; since y = 2 > 0 at x = 0, $f(x) = 2e^{x - x^{2}/2}$, for all real x (1 point for using the initial condition and solving for y).
parts.n: Writing $y = e^{x - x^{2}/2} + 2$ (adding the constant after exponentiating) earns only the first two points. Work with no constant of integration earns at most the separation point.

parts.q: Find d²y/dx² in terms of x and y. Is the approximation found in part (a) an overestimate or an underestimate of f(1)? Justify your answer.
parts.a: d²y/dx² = (dy/dx)(1 − x) − y = y(1 − x)² − y = y(x² − 2x) (1 point). From part (b), f(x) > 0 for every x, and x² − 2x = x(x − 2) < 0 for 0 < x < 1, so d²y/dx² < 0 on that interval. The graph of f is concave down there and lies below its tangent segments, so the Euler approximation 3.75 is an overestimate of f(1) (1 point).
parts.n: 'Overestimate, because f is increasing' earns no justification point: increasing does not decide which side of a tangent line the graph is on. Checking the sign of d²y/dx² only at x = 0, where it is 0, justifies nothing; the sign must hold on the whole interval.

parts.q: A student writes: "At x = 1, dy/dx = f(1)(1 − 1) = 0, and dy/dx changes from positive to negative there, so f has a relative maximum at x = 1. By part (a), that maximum value is 3.75." Is the student's reasoning correct? If not, correct it and give the maximum value of f. Justify your answer.
parts.a: The first sentence is correct, but the value is not (1 point for finding the error): 3.75 is an Euler approximation of f(1), and by part (c) it is too large. Because f(x) > 0, f′(x) = f(x)(1 − x) is positive for x < 1 and negative for x > 1, so f has its relative and absolute maximum at x = 1, and the maximum value is f(1) = $2e^{1/2}$ = 2√e (1 point, with this justification).
parts.n: Agreeing with the student earns nothing. 'Maximum at x = 1 because dy/dx = 0' with no sign change or second-derivative test earns no justification; a value read from the Euler table is never the exact maximum.

fr.title: A coasting cyclist: a drag model, a distance and a claim about stopping
fr.stem:
A cyclist stops pedaling at time t = 0 and coasts along a straight, flat road. Her speed v(t), in meters per second, decreases at a rate proportional to the square of her speed, where t is measured in seconds. At t = 0 her speed is 10 meters per second, and it is decreasing at 0.4 meter per second per second.
A calculator is not allowed. Part (d) uses an improper integral, which is BC only.

parts.q: Write a differential equation for v, and find the value of the constant of proportionality.
parts.a: dv/dt = −kv², with k > 0 (1 point). At t = 0, −0.4 = −k(10)², so k = 0.004, and dv/dt = −0.004v² (1 point).
parts.n: dv/dt = −kv (rate proportional to the speed, not its square) earns nothing; dividing 0.4 by 10 instead of 100 gives k = 0.04 and loses the second point. A positive right side says the cyclist speeds up and earns nothing.

parts.q: Find v(t), the particular solution to the differential equation from part (a) with v(0) = 10.
parts.a: Separate the variables: $v^{-2}\,dv = -0.004\,dt$ (1 point). Antidifferentiate: −1/v = −0.004t + C (1 point). At t = 0, −1/10 = C, so 1/v = 0.004t + 0.1, and $v(t) = \frac{1}{0.004t + 0.1} = \frac{250}{t + 25}$ for t ≥ 0 (1 point).
parts.n: Antidifferentiating v⁻² as v⁻³/(−3) (the derivative rule instead of the power rule for antiderivatives) earns only the separation point. A formula that is not solved for v, or that uses v(0) = 10 before a constant appears, loses the last point.

parts.q: Find the time at which the cyclist's speed is 5 meters per second, and find the distance she travels from t = 0 to that time.
parts.a: 250/(t + 25) = 5 gives t + 25 = 50, so t = 25 seconds (1 point). Because v > 0, distance = $\int_{0}^{25} \frac{250}{t + 25}\,dt$ = 250 ln(t + 25) evaluated from 0 to 25 = 250 ln(50/25) = 250 ln 2 meters, about 173 meters (1 point).
parts.n: Distance = speed × time, such as 5(25) = 125 or the average speed (10 + 5)/2 times 25 = 187.5, treats the speed as constant or as linear and earns only the time point.

parts.q: A student says, "Her speed approaches 0 as t increases, so according to this model she coasts only a limited total distance." Do you agree? Justify your answer.
parts.a: No (1 point for disagreeing with a reason from the model). The total distance is the improper integral $\int_{0}^{\infty} \frac{250}{t + 25}\,dt = \lim_{b \to \infty} 250\ln\left(\frac{b + 25}{25}\right)$, which increases without bound, so the integral diverges: the model predicts that she travels farther than any fixed distance, even though v → 0 (1 point). Her speed shrinks only like 250/t, too slowly for the distance to converge; a speed that tends to 0 is necessary for a finite distance but not sufficient.
parts.n: Agreeing because v → 0 earns nothing: that is the flaw in the student's reasoning. 'She never stops, so the distance is infinite' also earns nothing for the justification: under dv/dt = −kv the speed never reaches 0 either, yet the distance is finite.

u8.intro: Multiple-choice questions 17-24 and free-response question 1 allow a graphing calculator; all other questions are no calculator.

mc.stem:
Questions 1-3 refer to the following.

A particle moves along the x-axis. Its velocity v(t), for 0 ≤ t ≤ 8, is given by a graph made of two pieces:
• for 0 ≤ t ≤ 4, a semicircle below the t-axis, with endpoints (0, 0) and (4, 0) and lowest point (2, −2);
• for 4 ≤ t ≤ 8, the line segment from (4, 0) to (8, 4).
At time t = 0 the particle is at x = 1.

parts.q:
At what time t is the particle farthest to the left, and what is its position then?
(A) t = 2, and x = 1 − π
(B) t = 4, and x = −2π
(C) t = 4, and x = 1 − 2π
(D) t = 4, and x = 1 − 4π
parts.a: (C). The particle moves left while v < 0 (0 < t < 4) and right while v > 0 (4 < t < 8), so it is farthest left at t = 4. The semicircle has radius 2, so the area between it and the t-axis is (1/2)π(2)² = 2π, and x(4) = 1 − 2π. (A) stops at t = 2, where v is least: the particle is moving left fastest there, but it keeps moving left until v = 0 at t = 4 (x(2) = 1 − π). (B) reports the displacement −2π and forgets the starting position x(0) = 1. (D) uses the area of the whole circle, π(2)² = 4π, instead of half of it.
parts.n: CHA-4.C.1 (topic 8.2); skill 2.B. Thinking: the particle turns around where v changes sign, and position there is the initial position plus the signed area. Trap: (A), the time of greatest speed.

parts.q:
What is the average speed of the particle over the interval 0 ≤ t ≤ 8?
(A) 1 − π/4
(B) 1 + π/4
(C) 2
(D) 1 + π/2
parts.a: (B). Speed is |v(t)|, so its average is (1/8)∫₀⁸ |v(t)| dt, the total distance divided by the time. The distance is 2π (moving left) plus 8 (moving right, the triangle (1/2)(4)(4)), so the average speed is (8 + 2π)/8 = 1 + π/4. (A) is the average velocity, (8 − 2π)/8: it lets the leftward motion cancel part of the rightward motion. (C) averages the least and greatest speeds, 0 and 4; that is the average of a function only when the function is linear. (D) uses the area of a whole circle, 4π, for the semicircle: (8 + 4π)/8.
parts.n: CHA-4.B.1 (topic 8.1) with CHA-4.C.1 (topic 8.2); skill 1.E. Thinking: average value of |v| means total distance over time, not displacement over time. Trap: (A), the average velocity.

parts.q:
A student says, "After t = 4 the particle must move 2π units to the right to get back to x = 1. On 4 ≤ t ≤ 8 its average speed is 2, so it gets back to x = 1 at t = 4 + π." Which of the following best evaluates the student's reasoning?
(A) It is correct: at an average speed of 2 units per unit of time, moving 2π units takes π units of time.
(B) It is wrong: the particle cannot get back to x = 1 by t = 8, since its displacement on [0, 8] is negative.
(C) It is wrong: the particle gets back to x = 1 at t = 8, when the areas above and below the t-axis balance.
(D) It is wrong: for t ≥ 4, v(t) = t − 4, so by time T it has moved (T − 4)²/2, which is 2π at T = 4 + 2√π.
parts.a: (D). On 4 ≤ t ≤ 8 the velocity is the line v(t) = t − 4, so the distance moved right by time T is the triangle area (1/2)(T − 4)(T − 4). Setting (T − 4)²/2 = 2π gives T − 4 = √(4π) = 2√π, so T = 4 + 2√π ≈ 7.54, which is inside [4, 8]. The student's average speed of 2 belongs to the whole interval [4, 8]; the particle moves slowly at first, so it needs longer than π (T ≈ 7.14 is too early). (A) applies an average rate to only part of the interval. (B) misjudges the areas: the displacement on [0, 8] is 8 − 2π ≈ 1.72 > 0, so the particle ends to the right of x = 1 and must pass it. (C) assumes the two areas are equal; they are 2π ≈ 6.28 and 8, so the particle is back at x = 1 before t = 8.
parts.n: CHA-4.C.1 (topic 8.2); skill 3.E. Thinking: find the time at which an accumulated area reaches a target, instead of dividing by an average rate. Trap: (A), the average speed over the whole interval.

parts.q:
The graphs of f(x) = x³ and g(x) = 4x² − 3x intersect at x = 0, x = 1 and x = 3, and they enclose two regions. A student finds the total area of the two regions as |∫₀³ (x³ − 4x² + 3x) dx| = |−9/4| = 9/4. Which of the following best evaluates the student's work?
(A) It is wrong: f > g on 0 < x < 1 and g > f on 1 < x < 3, so the integral nets 5/12 against −8/3; the area is 37/12.
(B) It is correct: the absolute value turns the signed integral into an area, whichever curve is on top.
(C) It is wrong: g is above f on most of [0, 3], so the area is only the larger region, ∫₁³ (g − f) dx = 8/3.
(D) It is wrong: because the curves cross each other twice, the area must be found with an integral with respect to y instead.
parts.a: (A). f − g = x(x − 1)(x − 3), which is positive on (0, 1) (at x = 1/2 it is 5/8) and negative on (1, 3). The single integral adds 5/12 (region 1) and −8/3 (region 2), so the regions partly cancel before the absolute value is taken. The total area is 5/12 + 8/3 = 37/12, which is also the integral of |f − g| from 0 to 3. (B) takes the absolute value of the sum instead of the sum of the absolute values; that works only when the curves do not cross. (C) sees the crossing but drops the region between x = 0 and x = 1. (D) is a misconception: crossing curves call for splitting the x-interval at the crossings, not for changing the variable.
parts.n: CHA-5.A.3 (topic 8.6); skill 3.G. Thinking: find which curve is on top between each pair of intersections, then add the separate areas. Trap: (B), the absolute value of a signed total.

mc.stem:
Questions 5-6 refer to the following.

Let R be the region bounded by the graph of y = x², the x-axis and the line x = 3. Solid A has base R, and its cross sections perpendicular to the x-axis are squares. Solid B also has base R, but its cross sections perpendicular to the y-axis are squares.

parts.q:
A student says that solids A and B must have the same volume, because they have the same base and both have square cross sections. Which of the following best evaluates the claim?
(A) It is correct: each volume is the integral of the square of the width of R, and R has the same area either way.
(B) It is wrong: the squares perpendicular to the y-axis have side √y, so B has volume 81/2, less than A's 243/5.
(C) It is wrong: R is 9 units tall but only 3 units wide, so B, sliced along the taller direction, has more volume.
(D) It is wrong: A has volume 243/5, but B's squares have side 3 − √y, so B has volume ∫₀⁹ (3 − √y)² dy = 27/2.
parts.a: (D). For A, the square at x has side x², so V_A = ∫₀³ x⁴ dx = 243/5. For B, the horizontal segment across R at height y runs from x = √y to x = 3, so its length is 3 − √y and V_B = ∫₀⁹ (9 − 6√y + y) dy = 81 − 108 + 81/2 = 27/2. The squares of B are large only near the bottom of R, where R is wide, so B is much smaller. (A) confuses the area of R, which is the same either way, with the integral of the squared widths, which is not. (B) measures the width from the y-axis to the curve, √y; that segment lies outside R, which is to the right of the curve. (C) assumes a longer interval of integration means a larger volume; the squares perpendicular to the y-axis are small over most of that interval.
parts.n: CHA-5.B.1 (topic 8.7); skill 3.G. Thinking: find the side of each square from the direction of slicing, and see that the same base can give different volumes. Trap: (B), the width measured from the wrong side of the curve.

parts.q:
Solid C also has base R, but its cross sections perpendicular to the x-axis are semicircles whose diameters lie in R. What is the volume of solid C?
(A) 9π/8
(B) 243π/40
(C) 243π/20
(D) 243π/10
parts.a: (B). The diameter of the semicircle at x is x², so its radius is x²/2 and its area is (1/2)π(x²/2)² = πx⁴/8. Then V = (π/8)∫₀³ x⁴ dx = (π/8)(243/5) = 243π/40, which is π/8 times the volume of solid A. (A) uses the diameter x² instead of its square: (π/8)∫₀³ x² dx = 9π/8. (C) uses a whole circle of diameter x², area π(x²/2)² = πx⁴/4. (D) treats x² as the radius instead of the diameter: (1/2)π(x²)² = πx⁴/2.
parts.n: CHA-5.B.3 (topic 8.8); skill 1.E. Thinking: turn the new cross-section shape into an area in terms of x, then integrate over the same base. Trap: (D), the diameter used as the radius.

mc.stem:
Questions 7-9 refer to the following.

Let R be the region bounded by the graph of y = 2x − x² and the x-axis. The graph is a parabola that crosses the x-axis at x = 0 and x = 2 and has its highest point at (1, 1).

parts.q:
A student writes the volume of the solid formed when R is revolved about the line y = −1 as π∫₀² (2x − x² + 1)² dx. Which of the following best evaluates the student's integral?
(A) It is correct: the distance from the line y = −1 up to the curve is 2x − x² + 1, and that distance is the radius.
(B) It is wrong: the radius is 2x − x² − 1, because the line y = −1 is below the x-axis.
(C) It is wrong: the radius (2x − x² + 1) − 1 simplifies to 2x − x², so the volume is π∫₀² (2x − x²)² dx.
(D) It is wrong: it also counts the space between y = −1 and the x-axis; the volume is π∫₀² [(2x − x² + 1)² − 1] dx.
parts.a: (D). R does not touch the line y = −1: between the axis and R lies a strip of height 1, so each slice is a washer with outer radius (2x − x²) − (−1) = 2x − x² + 1 and inner radius 0 − (−1) = 1. The student's discs fill in the hole, adding a cylinder of radius 1 and length 2 (volume 2π): the student gets 86π/15 instead of 56π/15. (A) has the outer radius right but forgets the inner radius. (B) subtracts the axis in the wrong direction: the distance from y = −1 up to y = f(x) is f(x) − (−1). (C) subtracts the radii before squaring, π(R − r)² instead of π(R² − r²); that gives the volume about the x-axis, 16π/15.
parts.n: CHA-5.C.4 (topic 8.12); skill 3.G. Thinking: check whether the region touches the axis, and if not, find both radii from the axis. Trap: (C), squaring the difference of the radii.

parts.q:
Let V₋₁ be the volume of the solid formed when R is revolved about the line y = −1, and let V₂ be the volume when R is revolved about the line y = 2. Which of the following is true?
(A) V₂ > V₋₁, because V₂ = π∫₀² [2² − (2 − (2x − x²))²] dx = 64π/15 and V₋₁ = 56π/15.
(B) V₂ = V₋₁, because each line is exactly 1 unit from the nearest point of R, so the solids have the same holes.
(C) V₋₁ > V₂, because most of the area of R lies near the x-axis, which is the side of R closer to the line y = −1.
(D) V₂ > V₋₁, because V₂ = π∫₀² [2² − (2x − x²)²] dx = 104π/15 and V₋₁ = 56π/15.
parts.a: (A). About y = 2 the outer radius reaches down to the x-axis, 2 − 0 = 2, and the inner radius reaches the curve, 2 − (2x − x²). So V₂ = π∫₀² [4 − (2 − f)²] dx = π∫₀² (4f − f²) dx = π(16/3 − 16/15) = 64π/15, where f = 2x − x². About y = −1, V₋₁ = π∫₀² [(f + 1)² − 1] dx = π∫₀² (f² + 2f) dx = 56π/15. So V₂ is larger. (B) assumes equal gaps give equal volumes; the region is wide at the bottom and narrow at the top, so it is not placed the same way relative to each line. (C) has the geometry backwards: because most of R lies near the x-axis, most of R is far from the line y = 2, and material far from the axis sweeps out more volume. (D) reaches the right comparison with a wrong integral: the inner radius about y = 2 is 2 − f, the distance from the axis to the curve, not f.
parts.n: CHA-5.C.4 (topic 8.12); skill 2.D. Thinking: set up both washer integrals, taking every radius as a distance from the axis, and compare. Trap: (B), 'the same gap, the same volume'.

parts.q:
Which of the following is NOT equal to the volume of the solid formed when R is revolved about the y-axis?
(A) π∫₀¹ [(1 + √(1 − y))² − (1 − √(1 − y))²] dy
(B) 4π∫₀¹ √(1 − y) dy
(C) π∫₀¹ (2√(1 − y))² dy
(D) 8π/3
parts.a: (C). Solving y = 2x − x² for x gives x = 1 ± √(1 − y), so a horizontal slice at height y is a washer about the y-axis with outer radius 1 + √(1 − y) and inner radius 1 − √(1 − y): that is (A). Expanding, (1 + s)² − (1 − s)² = 4s with s = √(1 − y), which gives (B), and 4π∫₀¹ √(1 − y) dy = 4π(2/3) = 8π/3, which is (D). (C) squares the width of the slice, 2√(1 − y), as if π(R − r)² were the area of a washer; it equals 4π∫₀¹ (1 − y) dy = 2π, not 8π/3. (A), (B) and (D) are three forms of the same correct volume, so each of them is equal to it.
parts.n: CHA-5.C.3 (topic 8.11); skill 2.D. Thinking: write the washer in y, then check which expressions are rewritings of it. Trap: (B), which looks unfamiliar but is the expanded integrand.

parts.q:
Let R be the region bounded by the graph of y = √x, the line y = 2 − x and the x-axis. The graph and the line meet at (1, 1). Two students write the area of R.
Student 1: ∫₀¹ √x dx + ∫₁² (2 − x) dx
Student 2: ∫₀¹ (2 − y − y²) dy
Which of the following is true?
(A) Only Student 1 is correct: a region that rests on the x-axis must be sliced perpendicular to the x-axis.
(B) Both are correct: Student 1 splits R at x = 1, where its top boundary changes, and Student 2 uses horizontal strips.
(C) Only Student 2 is correct: Student 1 should have used the single integral ∫₀² (2 − x − √x) dx instead.
(D) Neither is correct: Student 2's strips run from x = 2 − y on the left to x = y² on the right, so the integrand must be y² − (2 − y).
parts.a: (B). R lies under y = √x for 0 ≤ x ≤ 1 and under y = 2 − x for 1 ≤ x ≤ 2, so vertical strips need two integrals: 2/3 + 1/2 = 7/6. A horizontal strip at height y (0 ≤ y ≤ 1) runs from the curve, x = y², on the left to the line, x = 2 − y, on the right, so Student 2's integral is right too: 2 − 1/2 − 1/3 = 7/6. (A) invents a rule; either direction of slicing works if each strip is measured correctly. (C) subtracts the curve from the line over [0, 2], which is the signed area between the two graphs, not R; it gives about 0.114. (D) has left and right reversed: at y = 1/2, x = y² = 1/4 is on the left and x = 2 − y = 3/2 is on the right.
parts.n: CHA-5.A.2 (topic 8.5); skill 3.G. Thinking: check each set-up against the region, measuring strips from left to right or from bottom to top. Trap: (C), the single integral in x.

parts.q:
A continuous function f has average value 5 on the interval [0, 4] and average value 2 on the interval [4, 10]. A student says that the average value of f on [0, 10] is (5 + 2)/2 = 3.5. Which of the following best evaluates the student's answer?
(A) It is correct: the average value on the whole interval is the average of the average values on its two pieces.
(B) It is wrong: the longer piece should count more, so the average value is (4 · 2 + 6 · 5)/10 = 3.8.
(C) It is wrong: the average value of f on [0, 10] cannot be found without a formula for f(x).
(D) It is wrong: ∫₀⁴ f(x) dx = 20 and ∫₄¹⁰ f(x) dx = 12, so the average value on [0, 10] is 32/10 = 3.2.
parts.a: (D). An average value times the length of its interval is the integral over that interval: ∫₀⁴ f(x) dx = 4(5) = 20 and ∫₄¹⁰ f(x) dx = 6(2) = 12. So ∫₀¹⁰ f(x) dx = 32, and the average value on [0, 10] is 32/10 = 3.2. (A) weights the two pieces equally, but [4, 10] is longer than [0, 4]. (B) has the right idea, weighting by length, but attaches each average to the other interval's length. (C) overlooks that the two averages already give the two integrals, which is all the average value needs.
parts.n: CHA-4.B.1 (topic 8.1); skill 3.G. Thinking: turn each average value back into an integral, add, and divide by the whole length. Trap: (A), averaging the averages.

parts.q:
Let R be the unbounded region in the first quadrant under the graph of y = 1/x for x ≥ 1. A student says, "The area of R is infinite, so the solid formed by revolving R about the x-axis must have infinite volume too." Which of the following best evaluates the claim? (Improper integrals are BC only.)
(A) It is wrong: the volume is $\pi\int_{1}^{\infty} \frac{1}{x^{2}}\,dx = \pi$, which converges although the area integral diverges.
(B) It is correct: the discs have radius 1/x, and $\int_{1}^{\infty} \frac{1}{x}\,dx$ diverges, so the volume integral must diverge too.
(C) It is wrong: the volume is $\pi\int_{1}^{\infty} \frac{1}{x^{2}}\,dx$, and an antiderivative of x⁻² is x⁻³/(−3), so it is π/3.
(D) It is wrong: the volume must be finite, because the radius 1/x of the discs approaches 0 as x increases.
parts.a: (A). Each disc has radius 1/x, so the volume is $\pi\int_{1}^{\infty} x^{-2}\,dx = \lim_{b \to \infty} \pi\left(1 - \frac{1}{b}\right) = \pi$. The area is $\int_{1}^{\infty} \frac{1}{x}\,dx = \lim_{b \to \infty} \ln b$, which diverges. Squaring the radius makes the integrand shrink fast enough (like 1/x²) for the volume to converge. (B) uses the radius, not the square of the radius, in the volume integral. (C) has the right integral but lowers the exponent, as the derivative rule does, instead of raising it: an antiderivative of x⁻² is −x⁻¹, not x⁻³/(−3). (D) gives a reason that proves nothing: the height 1/x of the region also approaches 0, yet the area is infinite; the rate at which the integrand shrinks decides convergence.
parts.n: CHA-5.C.1 (topic 8.9), with improper integrals from unit 6 (BC only); skill 3.G. Thinking: set up the disc integral and test its convergence separately from the area's. Trap: (D), 'the radius goes to 0, so it is finite'.

mc.stem:
Questions 13-14 refer to the following.

Let L be the length of the graph of y = x² from the point (0, 0) to the point (1, 1). Arc length is BC only. A student finds L as follows.
L = ∫₀¹ √(1 + (2x)²) dx = ∫₀¹ (1 + 2x) dx = [x + x²] from 0 to 1 = 2

parts.q:
Which of the following best evaluates the student's work?
(A) The set-up is wrong: the arc length integrand is √(1 + y²), so L = ∫₀¹ √(1 + x⁴) dx.
(B) The set-up is right, but √(1 + 4x²) ≠ 1 + 2x; since (1 + 2x)² = 1 + 4x + 4x², the value 2 is too large.
(C) The work is right: √(a² + b²) = a + b whenever a and b are positive, and here both 1 and 2x are positive on [0, 1].
(D) The set-up is wrong: the arc length integrand is √(1 + y′), so L = ∫₀¹ √(1 + 2x) dx.
parts.a: (B). The set-up is correct: y′ = 2x, so L = ∫₀¹ √(1 + 4x²) dx. The error is the next step. A square root does not split over a sum: (1 + 2x)² = 1 + 4x + 4x², which is larger than 1 + 4x² for x > 0, so 1 + 2x > √(1 + 4x²) and the student's value 2 is too large. (In fact L ≈ 1.479.) (A) puts the function itself in place of its derivative. (C) states a false rule; for example √(3² + 4²) = 5, not 7. (D) forgets to square the derivative.
parts.n: CHA-6.A.1 (topic 8.13, BC only); skill 3.G. Thinking: check the set-up and each algebra step, then decide which way the error moved the result. Trap: (C), the square root of a sum split into a sum.

parts.q:
Without evaluating the integral, which of the following must be true about L?
