(A) √2 < L < 2: no path from (0, 0) to (1, 1) is shorter than the segment, and each piece of this rising curve is shorter than its run plus rise.
(B) L < √2: the graph of y = x² lies below the segment from (0, 0) to (1, 1) for 0 < x < 1, so it takes a shorter route between the points.
(C) 2 < L < √5: the curve is longer than its run plus its rise, and the integrand √(1 + 4x²) is never more than √5 on the interval [0, 1].
(D) L = 2: the graph rises 1 unit while it runs 1 unit, and the length of any rising curve is exactly its run plus its rise.
parts.a: (A). The segment from (0, 0) to (1, 1) has length √2, and no curve joining the two points is shorter, so L > √2 (the curve is not that segment). On a small piece of the graph with run Δx and rise Δy > 0, the length is about √(Δx² + Δy²), which is less than Δx + Δy; adding the pieces, L < 1 + 1 = 2. (L ≈ 1.479.) (B) confuses lying below the segment with being shorter than it; the curve bends away from the straight path, so it is longer. (C) reverses the inequality between √(Δx² + Δy²) and Δx + Δy; the bound √5 is true but the lower bound 2 is not. (D) is the student's value from question 13; run plus rise is an upper bound, reached only by a path along the grid lines.
parts.n: CHA-6.A.1 (topic 8.13, BC only); skill 1.F. Thinking: bound an arc length from below by the chord and from above by run plus rise. Trap: (B), 'below the chord, so shorter'.

mc.stem:
Questions 15-16 refer to the following.

A museum opens at t = 0 and closes at t = 10, where t is measured in hours. At t = 0 there are already 100 people inside (staff and a school group). The number of people inside is N(t), and it changes at a rate of r(t) people per hour, where r is continuous. The graph of r is described as follows.
• r(t) > 0 for 0 < t < 3, r(t) < 0 for 3 < t < 7, and r(t) > 0 for 7 < t < 10; r has its least value at t = 5.
• The region between the graph of r and the t-axis has area 50 for 0 ≤ t ≤ 3, area 80 for 3 ≤ t ≤ 7, and area 20 for 7 ≤ t ≤ 10.

parts.q:
At what time t, for 0 ≤ t ≤ 10, is the number of people in the museum least?
(A) t = 3
(B) t = 5
(C) t = 7
(D) t = 10
parts.a: (C). N decreases only while r < 0, on 3 < t < 7, so the least value is at t = 7 or at an endpoint. N(0) = 100, N(7) = 100 + 50 − 80 = 70, and N(10) = 70 + 20 = 90. The least number is 70, at t = 7. (A) is where r changes from positive to negative: N is greatest there, N(3) = 150. (B) is where r is least: N is falling fastest at t = 5, but it keeps falling until t = 7. (D) is the closing time; N rises on 7 < t < 10, so N(10) = 90 is above N(7).
parts.n: CHA-4.D.1, CHA-4.D.2 (topic 8.3); skill 2.B. Thinking: use the sign of the rate to find candidates and the areas to compare them. Trap: (B), the time the number falls fastest.

parts.q:
The manager says, "The rate r(t) was positive for 6 of the 10 hours, so there were more people in the museum at closing time than at opening time." Which of the following best evaluates the manager's claim?
(A) It is correct: people arrived faster than they left during most of the day, so the number inside rose over the day.
(B) It is correct: N(10) = 100 + 50 + 80 + 20 = 250, which is far more than the 100 people at opening time.
(C) It cannot be decided: the areas alone do not determine N(10) unless a formula for r(t) is also known.
(D) It is wrong: N(10) = 100 + 50 − 80 + 20 = 90; the net change is the signed area, not the time r is positive.
parts.a: (D). The net change in N over [0, 10] is ∫₀¹⁰ r(t) dt, the area above the t-axis minus the area below it: 50 − 80 + 20 = −10. So N(10) = 90, fewer than at opening. How long r is positive does not matter; how much area lies on each side does. (A) counts hours instead of people: the 4 hours of loss removed more people (80) than the 6 hours of gain added (70). (B) adds every area as a gain; 250 is the total number of arrivals and departures counted together, not the net change. (C) overlooks that the Fundamental Theorem needs only the integral of r, which the signed areas give.
parts.n: CHA-4.D.2, CHA-4.E.1 (topic 8.3); skill 3.F. Thinking: net change is the signed area under the rate. Trap: (A), counting hours of gain instead of people.

mc.stem:
Questions 17-18 refer to the following.

Water flows into a tank at a rate of W(t) = 20 + 15 sin(0.5t) liters per minute, and water drains out of the tank at a rate of D(t) = 3t + 4 liters per minute, for 0 ≤ t ≤ 10 minutes. At time t = 0 the tank holds 200 liters. A graphing calculator is allowed.

parts.q:
How much water is in the tank at time t = 10 minutes?
(A) 31.490 liters
(B) 216.541 liters
(C) 231.490 liters
(D) 421.490 liters
parts.a: (C). The amount at t = 10 is the starting amount plus the net change: 200 + ∫₀¹⁰ (W(t) − D(t)) dt ≈ 200 + 221.490 − 190 = 231.490 liters. (A) is the net change alone, without the 200 liters already in the tank. (B) comes from evaluating sin(0.5t) in degree mode; the model is in radians. (D) adds all the water that flowed in but ignores the water that drained out.
parts.n: CHA-4.D.2, CHA-4.E.1 (topic 8.3); skill 1.E. Thinking: amount = initial amount + integral of (rate in − rate out). Trap: (A), the net change reported as the amount.

parts.q:
A student says the tank holds the most water at t = π ≈ 3.142 minutes, because that is when water flows in fastest. Which of the following best evaluates the claim?
(A) It is wrong: the amount rises while W(t) > D(t), which lasts until t ≈ 6.011, when the tank holds its most, about 301.700 liters.
(B) It is correct: the amount of water grows fastest when the inflow W(t) is greatest, so it is greatest at that time.
(C) It is wrong: the amount is greatest at t = 10, because more water flows in than drains out over 0 ≤ t ≤ 10.
(D) It is wrong: the amount is greatest at t ≈ 6.011, because the rate W(t) − D(t) reaches its greatest value there.
parts.a: (A). The amount A(t) has A′(t) = W(t) − D(t), which is positive until W(t) = D(t) at t ≈ 6.011 (found with the calculator) and negative after, so A has its maximum there. Candidates: A(0) = 200, A(6.011) = 200 + $\int_{0}^{6.011} (W(t) - D(t))\,dt$ ≈ 301.700, A(10) ≈ 231.490. At t = π the amount is only about 265.461: the inflow is greatest then, but the amount is still rising because W > D. (B) confuses the greatest rate of inflow with the greatest amount; the amount keeps growing as long as the net rate is positive. (C) uses the net change over the whole interval: the tank does end with more than it began, but it lost water after t ≈ 6.011, so t = 10 is not the maximum. (D) has the right time for the wrong reason: at t ≈ 6.011 the net rate W − D is 0, not greatest.
parts.n: CHA-4.D.1, CHA-4.E.1 (topic 8.3); skill 3.D. Thinking: find where the net rate changes sign and compare the candidates. Trap: (B), the peak of the inflow taken as the peak of the amount.

mc.stem:
Questions 19-20 refer to the following.

Let R be the region in the first quadrant enclosed by the graphs of $y = 3xe^{-x}$ and y = x/4. The graphs meet at the origin and at exactly one other point, and $3xe^{-x}$ > x/4 between them. A graphing calculator is allowed.

parts.q:
For what value of k does the vertical line x = k divide R into two regions of equal area?
(A) 1.000
(B) 1.013
(C) 1.242
(D) 1.248
parts.a: (B). The graphs meet where $3e^{-x} = \frac{1}{4}$, at x = ln 12 ≈ 2.485. The area of R is $\int_{0}^{\ln 12} \left(3xe^{-x} - \frac{x}{4}\right)dx$ ≈ 1.357. The line x = k splits it evenly when $\int_{0}^{k} \left(3xe^{-x} - \frac{x}{4}\right)dx$ ≈ 0.678, which the calculator solves as k ≈ 1.013. (A) assumes the line through the peak of y = 3xe^{−x} (at x = 1) splits R in half; the area to its left is about 0.668, a little short. (C) is halfway between x = 0 and x = ln 12; R is taller on the left, so halving the interval does not halve the area. (D) halves the area under y = 3xe^{−x} alone and forgets to subtract the region under y = x/4.
parts.n: CHA-5.A.1 (topic 8.4), with an accumulation function from unit 6; skill 1.E. Thinking: write the area to the left of x = k as a function of k and solve for half the total. Trap: (C), halving the interval.

parts.q:
A student finds the volume of the solid formed when R is revolved about the x-axis as $\pi\int_{0}^{\ln 12} \left(3xe^{-x} - \frac{x}{4}\right)^{2}dx$ ≈ 2.911. Which of the following best evaluates the student's work?
(A) It is correct: the radius of each slice is the vertical distance between the two graphs, 3xe⁻ˣ − x/4.
(B) It is wrong: the solid has no hole, so the volume is π times the integral of (3xe⁻ˣ)² from 0 to ln 12, about 6.169.
(C) It is wrong: the volume is the integral of (3xe⁻ˣ)² − (x/4)² from 0 to ln 12, about 1.644.
(D) It is wrong: each slice is a washer, so the volume is π times the integral of (3xe⁻ˣ)² − (x/4)² from 0 to ln 12, about 5.165.
parts.a: (D). R does not reach the x-axis except at the origin: below R lies the region under y = x/4. Each slice is a washer with outer radius 3xe⁻ˣ and inner radius x/4, so $V = \pi\int_{0}^{\ln 12} \left(9x^{2}e^{-2x} - \frac{x^{2}}{16}\right)dx$ ≈ 5.165. The student squared the difference of the radii, and (R − r)² < R² − r² when 0 < r < R, so 2.911 is too small. (A) treats the gap between the graphs as a radius; a radius is measured from the axis of revolution. (B) fills in the hole: it revolves the whole region under y = 3xe⁻ˣ. (C) has the right washers but leaves out the factor π.
parts.n: CHA-5.C.3 (topic 8.11); skill 3.G. Thinking: measure both radii from the axis, and compare π(R² − r²) with π(R − r)². Trap: (A), the gap between the curves used as a radius.

parts.q:
A section of a roller-coaster track follows the graph of y = 10 + 5 sin(x/4) for 0 ≤ x ≤ 25, where x and y are measured in meters. What is the length of this section of track? (Arc length is BC only.)
(A) 25.001 meters
(B) 32.907 meters
(C) 39.971 meters
(D) 84.899 meters
parts.a: (B). y′ = (5/4)cos(x/4), so the length is $\int_{0}^{25} \sqrt{1 + \left(1.25\cos\frac{x}{4}\right)^{2}}\,dx$ ≈ 32.907 meters. (A) is the straight-line distance between the ends of the track, from (0, 10) to (25, 9.834); the track is longer because it rises and falls. (C) evaluates the cosine in degree mode, where cos(x/4) stays near 1, so every piece looks steep. (D) differentiates 5 sin(x/4) as 5 cos(x/4), leaving out the chain-rule factor 1/4.
parts.n: CHA-6.A.1 (topic 8.13, BC only); skill 1.E. Thinking: differentiate carefully, build the arc-length integrand, and check the answer against the straight-line distance. Trap: (D), the missing chain-rule factor.

parts.q:
The temperature on a spring day is modeled by $T(t) = 55 + 20e^{-\left(\frac{t - 14}{5}\right)^{2}}$ degrees Fahrenheit, where t is hours after midnight and 0 ≤ t ≤ 24. What is the average temperature over the day, and at how many times in 0 < t < 24 is the temperature equal to that average?
(A) 62.368°F, reached at two times
(B) 62.368°F, reached at exactly one time
(C) 65.004°F, reached at two times
(D) 55.187°F, reached at exactly one time
parts.a: (A). The average value is $\frac{1}{24}\int_{0}^{24} T(t)\,dt$ ≈ 62.368°F. T rises from about 55.0 at t = 0 to 75 at t = 14 and falls to about 55.4 at t = 24, so it passes 62.368 once on the way up and once on the way down: at t ≈ 9.003 and t ≈ 18.997. (B) reads the Mean Value Theorem for integrals as 'exactly one time'; the theorem guarantees at least one. (C) averages the lowest and highest temperatures, (55.008 + 75)/2; that is not the average value of T over the day. (D) averages the temperatures at the two endpoints, T(0) and T(24); a function's average value depends on all its values, not just the ends.
parts.n: CHA-4.B.1 (topic 8.1); skill 2.B. Thinking: compute the average value with an integral, then use the shape of T to count where T equals it. Trap: (B), 'the theorem gives exactly one'.

parts.q:
A particle moves along the x-axis with velocity $v(t) = e^{\sin t} - 1.2$ for 0 ≤ t ≤ 6, and its position at time t = 0 is x = 0. What is the greatest value of the particle's position x(t) for 0 ≤ t ≤ 6?
(A) 0.508
(B) 1.219
(C) 2.458
(D) 2.477
parts.a: (C). v(t) = 0 where sin t = ln 1.2, at t ≈ 0.183 and t ≈ 2.958. The particle moves left on (0, 0.183), right on (0.183, 2.958), and left on (2.958, 6), so the candidates are x(0) = 0, x(2.958) and x(6). With the calculator, x(2.958) = $\int_{0}^{2.958} v(t)\,dt$ ≈ 2.458 and x(6) ≈ 0.508, so the greatest position is 2.458. (A) is x(6), the position at the end; the particle moves left after t ≈ 2.958. (B) is the position at t = π/2, where the velocity is greatest; the particle keeps moving right after that. (D) is the distance moved right on (0.183, 2.958); it forgets that the particle first moved slightly left, to x ≈ −0.019.
parts.n: CHA-4.C.1 (topic 8.2); skill 3.D. Thinking: find where v changes sign, then compare positions at those times and at the endpoints. Trap: (D), the rightward distance mistaken for the position.

parts.q:
Let R be the region bounded by the graph of y = ln x, the line y = 2 and the line x = 1. When R is revolved about the x-axis, the volume of the solid is 2π(e² − 1) ≈ 40.144. What is the volume of the solid formed when R is revolved about the line y = 2 instead?
(A) 8.304
(B) 13.789
(C) 15.011
(D) 40.144
parts.a: (C). R lies below y = 2 and above y = ln x, for 1 ≤ x ≤ e² (where ln x = 2). R touches the line y = 2 all along its top, so each slice is a disc of radius 2 − ln x, and $V = \pi\int_{1}^{e^{2}} (2 - \ln x)^{2}\,dx$ ≈ 15.011. (A) stops at x = 2, confusing the line y = 2 with the right edge of R. (B) forgets to square the radius: $\pi\int_{1}^{e^{2}} (2 - \ln x)\,dx$. (D) assumes the volume does not depend on the axis; about the x-axis, R is far from the axis and each slice is a washer with radii 2 and ln x, so the solid is much larger.
parts.n: CHA-5.C.2 (topic 8.10); skill 2.D. Thinking: moving the axis to the region's edge turns washers into discs with a new radius. Trap: (D), the same region taken to give the same volume.

fr.title: Solar panels and a battery: average use, stored energy and the fastest charge
fr.stem:
A school's solar panels generate electricity at a rate of $S(t) = 80\sin\left(\frac{\pi(t - 6)}{12}\right)$ kilowatts, and the school uses electricity at a rate of $U(t) = 25 + 20e^{-(t - 13)^{2}/8}$ kilowatts, where t is measured in hours after midnight and 6 ≤ t ≤ 18. A battery takes in the difference: the energy stored in the battery, B(t) kilowatt-hours, changes at the rate S(t) − U(t) kilowatts, and B(6) = 100.
A graphing calculator is allowed.

parts.q: Find the average rate at which the school uses electricity over 6 ≤ t ≤ 18. Must there be a time t, for 6 < t < 18, at which U(t) equals this average? Justify your answer.
parts.a: The average is $\frac{1}{12}\int_{6}^{18} U(t)\,dt$ ≈ 33.302 kilowatts (1 point). Yes. U is continuous, and U(6) ≈ 25.044 < 33.302 < 45 = U(13), so by the Intermediate Value Theorem there is a time t with 6 < t < 13 at which U(t) = 33.302 (1 point). (The calculator finds t ≈ 10.348, and also t ≈ 15.652.)
parts.n: An average found as (U(6) + U(18))/2 or as (25 + 45)/2 earns nothing. 'Yes, by the IVT' without values of U on both sides of 33.302 does not earn the justification point.

parts.q: Find B(18), the energy stored in the battery at t = 18 hours.
parts.n: Leaving out the initial 100 gives 211.536 and loses the answer point. Integrating S alone ignores the school's use and earns nothing.

parts.q: At what time t, for 6 ≤ t ≤ 18, is the energy stored in the battery greatest? Justify your answer.
parts.a: B′(t) = S(t) − U(t) = 0 at t ≈ 7.230 and t ≈ 16.582 (1 point). B′ < 0 on (6, 7.230), B′ > 0 on (7.230, 16.582) and B′ < 0 on (16.582, 18). Comparing the candidates, B(6) = 100, B(7.230) ≈ 84.784, B(16.582) ≈ 329.222 and B(18) ≈ 311.536 (1 point), the stored energy is greatest at t ≈ 16.582 hours, when it is about 329.222 kilowatt-hours (1 point, with the Candidates Test or the sign analysis as the justification).
parts.n: t = 12, the time of greatest sunlight, earns nothing: the battery keeps gaining energy as long as S > U. An answer of t ≈ 16.582 with no sign analysis or comparison with the endpoints earns only the first point.

parts.q: A student says, "The battery charges fastest at noon, t = 12, because that is when the panels generate the most electricity." Do you agree? Justify your answer.
parts.a: No (1 point for disagreeing with a reason from the model). The battery charges at the rate B′(t) = S(t) − U(t), which depends on the school's use as well as on the panels. B′ is greatest where S′(t) − U′(t) = 0, at t ≈ 10.882, where B′ ≈ 40.182 kilowatts; at t = 12, B′ = 80 − 42.650 ≈ 37.350 kilowatts, which is less, because the school's use is rising toward its peak at t = 13 (1 point).
parts.n: Agreeing earns nothing. 'It charges fastest when U is least' makes the same mistake from the other side. Comparing B′(12) with one other time, without locating the maximum of B′, earns only the first point.

fr.title: A region between a parabola and a line: area, washers about y = 4 and slices in y
fr.stem:
Let R be the region in the first quadrant bounded by the graph of y = 4 − x², the line y = 3x and the y-axis. The graph and the line meet at the point (1, 3).
A calculator is not allowed.

parts.q: Find the area of R.
parts.a: Area = ∫₀¹ [(4 − x²) − 3x] dx (1 point) = [4x − x³/3 − 3x²/2] from 0 to 1 = 4 − 1/3 − 3/2 = 13/6 (1 point).
parts.n: ∫₀¹ [3x − (4 − x²)] dx = −13/6 has the curves reversed, and reporting it loses the answer point. Integrating to x = 2, where the parabola meets the x-axis, includes area outside R.

parts.q: Find the volume of the solid formed when R is revolved about the horizontal line y = 4.
parts.a: The line y = 4 lies above R and touches it only at (0, 4). A vertical slice at x is a washer with outer radius 4 − 3x (from y = 4 down to the line) and inner radius 4 − (4 − x²) = x² (from y = 4 down to the parabola) (1 point for both radii). V = π∫₀¹ [(4 − 3x)² − (x²)²] dx (1 point) = π[16x − 12x² + 3x³ − x⁵/5] from 0 to 1 = π(16 − 12 + 3 − 1/5) = 34π/5 (1 point).
parts.n: Radii 4 − x² and 3x are distances from the x-axis; they give the volume about the x-axis and earn at most the integral's form. π∫₀¹ (4 − 3x − x²)² dx squares the difference of the radii and earns only the radii point.

parts.q: Write, but do not evaluate, an expression involving one or more integrals for the volume of the solid whose base is R and whose cross sections perpendicular to the y-axis are squares. Explain why your expression has the form it does.
parts.a: V = ∫₀³ (y/3)² dy + ∫₃⁴ (√(4 − y))² dy (1 point for each integral, with its side length and limits). A horizontal segment across R at height y runs from the y-axis to the right edge of R, and the right edge changes at (1, 3): for 0 ≤ y ≤ 3 it is the line, x = y/3, and for 3 ≤ y ≤ 4 it is the parabola, x = √(4 − y). So one integral is needed for each piece.
parts.n: The single integral ∫₀⁴ (√(4 − y) − y/3)² dy earns nothing: for y < 3 the segment from the line to the parabola lies outside R, and for y > 3 the line is not a boundary of R at all.

parts.q: A student says that the vertical line x = 1/2 divides R into two regions of equal area, because it is halfway between x = 0 and x = 1. Do you agree? Justify your answer.
parts.a: No (1 point). The area of R to the left of x = 1/2 is $\int_{0}^{1/2} (4 - x^{2} - 3x)\,dx$ = 2 − 1/24 − 3/8 = 19/12, which is more than half the area, 13/12 (1 point). R is 4 units tall at the y-axis and narrows to a point at x = 1, so more of its area lies on the left.
parts.n: Agreeing earns nothing. 'No, because R is not symmetric' with no area computed or compared earns only the first point.

fr.title: Particle motion: position, distance, the farthest point and two theorems
fr.stem:
A particle moves along the x-axis so that its velocity at time t, for 0 ≤ t ≤ 4, is v(t) = 3t² − 12t + 9, where t is measured in seconds and v(t) in meters per second. At time t = 0 the particle is at x = 2.
A calculator is not allowed.

parts.q: Find the position of the particle at time t = 4.
parts.a: x(4) = 2 + ∫₀⁴ (3t² − 12t + 9) dt (1 point) = 2 + [t³ − 6t² + 9t] from 0 to 4 = 2 + (64 − 96 + 36) = 6 meters (1 point).
parts.n: Leaving out the initial position gives 4, the displacement, and loses the answer point.

parts.q: Find the total distance the particle travels over the interval 0 ≤ t ≤ 4.
parts.a: v(t) = 3(t − 1)(t − 3), so v > 0 on (0, 1), v < 0 on (1, 3) and v > 0 on (3, 4) (1 point for splitting at t = 1 and t = 3). The distance is ∫₀¹ v dt − ∫₁³ v dt + ∫₃⁴ v dt = 4 + 4 + 4 = 12 meters (1 point).
parts.n: |∫₀⁴ v(t) dt| = 4 is the displacement, not the distance, and earns nothing.

parts.q: A student says, "The particle is farthest to the right at t = 4, and at no other time, because it is moving to the right at t = 4 and x(4) > x(0)." Is the student's reasoning correct? Justify your answer.
parts.a: No (1 point). The particle changes direction at t = 1 and t = 3, so the candidates for its rightmost position are t = 0, 1, 3 and 4: x(0) = 2, x(1) = 2 + 4 = 6, x(3) = 6 − 4 = 2 and x(4) = 2 + 4 = 6. The greatest position, 6, occurs at both t = 1 and t = 4 (1 point). Moving right at the end, and ending to the right of the start, does not rule out an earlier turning point that is just as far right.
parts.n: Agreeing earns nothing. 'Farthest right at t = 1' alone misses the tie at t = 4, and a conclusion with no positions computed earns only the first point.

parts.q: Find the average velocity and the average speed of the particle over 0 ≤ t ≤ 4. Must there be a time t, for 0 < t < 4, at which the velocity equals the average velocity? Must there be a time at which the speed equals the average speed? Justify your answers.
parts.a: Average velocity = (x(4) − x(0))/4 = 4/4 = 1 meter per second, and average speed = 12/4 = 3 meters per second (1 point). Velocity: x is differentiable, so it is continuous on [0, 4] and differentiable on (0, 4); by the Mean Value Theorem there is a c in (0, 4) with v(c) = x′(c) = 1 (1 point). Speed: |v(t)| is continuous, with |v(0)| = 9 > 3 and |v(1)| = 0 < 3, so by the Intermediate Value Theorem the speed equals 3 at some time in (0, 1) (1 point). (In fact v = 1 at t = 2 ± 2√3/3, and the speed is 3 at t = 2 − √2, 2 and 2 + √2.)
parts.n: Averaging v(0) and v(4) gives 9 and earns nothing. The Mean Value Theorem cannot be cited for the speed: it gives the average rate of change of position, which is the average velocity, not the average speed.
